text: With the federal election less than a year away, Miersch assumes the post at a critical moment for the struggling SPD. The party is now polling at 16 percent nationally, nearly 10 points below its result in the last federal election in 2021. In the June European election the SPD — which traces its roots back to Imperial Germany in the late nineteenth century — recorded its worst result in a national election in well over a century.  As general secretary, Miersch will serve as one of the chief defenders of the party and its policies, and help craft the SPD’s election message. Given Germany’s weak economy, that platform will likely rest on economic growth.  “We are firmly convinced that the upcoming Bundestag election will focus on economic and industrial policy,” Lars Klingbeil, one of the SPD’s national leaders, said on Tuesday.  Miersch, 55, has been an SPD parliamentarian for nearly two decades and was key in establishing the coalition’s gas price cap to shield consumers and companies from high energy costs after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. He also pushed for subsidies related to a controversial law to replace gas boilers with heat pumps.  Miersch takes on the role at a time when many question whether Scholz’s three-party ruling coalition — which has scuffled over everything from migration to spending — will survive until next September’s federal election.  “[Miersch] is facing a huge challenge, because the situation in the federal government is super tense and it’s not at all clear if the coalition will hold,” said Tim Klüssendorf, an SPD parliamentarian. “He has to organize an election campaign against the background of that uncertainty, without even being able to rely on an election date.”  The SPD’s previous general secretary, Kevin Kühnert, resigned on Monday citing health problems.

description: In short, Hezbollah was meant to be Lebanon’s protector from Israel. Nasrallah was the protector-in-chief; under his leadership, Hezbollah became the key reason Israel ended its 18-year occupation of southern Lebanon in 2000, worn down by the high casualties inflicted on the Israel Defense Forces.
text: Astonishingly scything through arch-foe Hezbollah’s upper echelons, remorselessly picking off leaders and military commanders one after another, Israel’s becoming increasingly bullish, convinced the disaster of Oct. 7 is being paid back.  Israel is being made safer, victory snatched from the jaws of defeat — or so its leaders argue. And soon, they believe, it will achieve the unbelievable — vanquishing both of Iran’s key allies in the region: Hamas and Hezbollah — the redrawing of the Middle East’s geopolitical map within its grasp.  Of course, how Israel’s military campaign actually fares — whether Iran and Hezbollah find a convenient hook to disengage, are thoroughly defeated on the battlefield or, as some fear, Israel is beckoned by a quagmire in the stony, ravine-filled terrain of southern Lebanon — only time will tell. But whatever happens, the cost in human misery and lives will be high. And as Israelis continue to mourn those murdered in Hamas’ slaughter of innocents, many are in no mood to think much about the human toll in Lebanon or Gaza.  But while it’s premature for Israel to celebrate its extraordinary military achievements, there can be no doubt that Iran and Hezbollah are on the back foot. And that is thanks to the miscalculations made by both Hezbollah’s now-dead leader of three decades, Hassan Nasrallah, and the mullahs in Tehran.  In Nasrallah’s case, the missteps cost him his life — as did his decision to remain in Lebanon, despite being urged to flee by Iran’s Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, his friend and backer.  “Already, Hezbollah has been greatly diminished,” said Paul Salem, former president of the Middle East Institute. “Hezbollah’s charismatic leader is gone; most of the leadership is gone; their communications are hit. They’ve lost their deterrent power against Israel, and they have no defense against Israel’s aerial attacks. Hezbollah’s raison d’être — defending the villages of the south — has gone too. They’ve all been evacuated,” he told POLITICO.

Rutte's comments came as he took part in a three-way talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer at No. 10 Downing Street as the Ukrainian leader embarks on a whistle-stop tour of Western capitals to push for extra support.  After the meeting, Rutte told journalists it would be “up to individual allies” to decide whether to approve the use of long-range missiles to hit targets inside Russia, as Zelenskyy has long been pushing for.  “Let's not focus on one weapon system,” he urged. “It will not be one weapon system which will make the change. I understand what Zelenskyy is asking, but at the same time he also agrees that there is a broader issue to be debated to make sure that they prevail.”  Starmer’s spokesman told journalists the leaders’ discussion focused on “how we help Ukraine be in the strongest position going forward at this crucial time.”  He said: “We obviously want to put Ukraine in the strongest position, but no war has ever been won by a single weapon."  Zelenskyy was due to unveil his “victory plan” at a meeting of senior NATO leaders at the weekend. Conservative opposition leadership contender James Cleverly — currently the shadow home secretary — said Wednesday that Cooper had “questions to answer” over the move.  “The SEG is dedicated to the very serious business of protecting the Royal Family, senior government ministers and foreign heads of state,” ex-Met commander John O’Connor told the Sun. “This is an abuse of an elite service.”  The move came after three of Swift’s earlier Vienna shows had to be cancelled after the CIA warned Austrian authorities about a planned terrorist attack. text: — Estonia’s Kaja Kallas pointed out it has been 13 years since she complied with transparency requirements attached to her various roles as an Estonian or EU official. “I have not declared any financial interest as I do not have any,” she writes to lawmakers, adding this comes as a result of a “conscious decision not to invest in any shares or bonds of companies or similar instruments” because of her functions.  The future chief of the EU’s foreign service arm, who faced controversy at home related to her husband’s investments, also said she and her husband have “thoroughly verified that it cannot be considered to be capable of giving rise to a conflict of interest.” Her husband owns a consultancy which also has shares in a company providing storage facilities. text: Cuba asked to join the BRICS group of emerging economies, senior foreign ministry official Carlos Miguel Pereira announced Tuesday.    “Cuba has officially requested its incorporation into the BRICS as a ‘Partner Country,’ through a letter to the President of Russia, Vladimir Putin, who holds the Presidency of the Group, which is consolidating as a key player in global geopolitics and hope for the countries of the South,” Pereira said on X.    Pereira’s overtures to Putin come two weeks before BRICS members meet at the bloc’s annual summit which is scheduled for Oct. 22-24 in the Russian city of Kazan.    The Caribbean country’s bid to join the bloc arrives shortly after Azerbaijan confirmed it is also pushing for membership, following a meeting between Putin and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev.    Membership of BRICS is invitation-only, and multiple countries were given the chance to join at the start of this year, including Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates. Argentina also received an invitation but said it won’t join.    BRICS was founded in 2009 to foster closer ties among Russia, China, India and Brazil, and now comprises nine members. It is becoming a geopolitical and economic rival to the Western bloc of G7 countries.  CORRECTION: This article has been updated to correct Carlos Miguel Pereira’s position at the foreign ministry.

description: PARIS — France and Italy are demanding answers from Israeli envoys after United Nations peacekeepers in south Lebanon were wounded in separate incidents on Thursday and Friday, amid Israel's expanding ground invasion of its northern neighbor targeting Hezbollah.. The two countries, which supply large amounts of troops to the U.N. peacekeeping mission in south Lebanon known as UNIFIL ...
text: The two soldiers who were hurt on Thursday were injured after an Israeli tank fired toward a UNIFIL observation tower. The duo who sustained injuries on Friday were wounded "after two explosions occurred close to an observation tower," UNIFIL said in a statement.  “This is a serious development, and UNIFIL reiterates that the safety and security of U.N. personnel and property must be guaranteed and that the inviolability of U.N. premises must be respected at all times,” UNIFIL said, adding that “any deliberate attack on peacekeepers is a grave violation of international humanitarian law.”  Italy summoned Israel's ambassador on Thursday, while France did so on Friday.  The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) responded on X to both incidents. On Thursday, it noted that Hezbollah operates near both civilian and UNIFIL positions and said it "maintains routine communication with UNIFIL." Responding to the reports of the two wounded soldiers on Friday, the IDF said in a statement that the incident took place when its soldiers responded to a "threat" located about 50 meters away from a UNIFIL post. The Israeli military added that it had "instructed UNIFIL personnel to enter into protected spaces and remain there."  But demanding that an international force dedicated to preserving peace in a geopolitical hotspot move to facilitate a military invasion is highly inflammatory. Irish President Michael Higgins called such a move "outrageous," while Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto on Thursday said the peacekeepers will stay where they are.  "We will never be the ones to move because someone tells us, by force, to move," Crosetto said.

text: TotalEnergies contracted a Mozambican security unit to defend the plant despite warnings that some soldiers had allegedly carried out human rights abuses. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images  Mozambique’s Defense Ministry expressed “total openness and willingness to accept a transparent and impartial investigation” into allegations of military violence at a natural gas facility operated by TotalEnergies.  POLITICO reported last month that a Mozambican military unit operating out of TotalEnergies’ gatehouse at the site in Cabo Delgado massacred and tortured dozens of civilians in 2021.  The soldiers accused villagers who had fled their homes of being members of an Islamist insurgency, then crammed them into shipping containers and subjected them to beatings and starvation over three months. Of those captured, only a small portion survived.

text: Ironically, it was Chemours itself that had conducted the tests under an agreement with the regional authorities.  Maintaining locals' trust was especially important to the company at the time as it was planning a €186 million expansion to start producing PFAS chemicals vital in manufacturing green hydrogen — a carbon-free fuel that is central to Europe's decarbonization plans and the global fight against climate change. If these potentially dangerous chemicals were polluting local food, it could put hydrogen's social licence in jeopardy.  "When we heard there were going to be huge investments [in the local factory] ... Everyone though that the project was very good news," the town's Deputy Mayor Alexandre Ouizille said in an interview, pointing to job creation and the benefit to the climate.  But after newspaper reports uncovered "the eternal pollution of PFAS," the mood changed, he said. It wasn't just the test results. In 2023, an investigation by newspaper Le Monde had revealed PFAS pollution in the area.  It prompted Ouizille's superior, local Mayor Gérard Weyn, to ask for the French environment ministry's input.  "Before the commune commits further to this project, your answers to our various precautionary questions are essential to dispel any doubts about the safety of the current facility and the proposed extension," he wrote in a letter, seen by POLITICO.

text: Democrats and Republicans are gearing up for the presidential election. As the geopolitical landscape has changed with the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the Middle East escalation, the quality of the EU-U.S. cooperation could tilt the global power balance. It’s not only geopolitics. The stakes are high for the EU on several fronts – economic competitiveness, climate agenda, defense capacity, trade relationship with China – and the bloc is closely watching who will sit in the Oval Office. How are Democrats and Republicans addressing these issues that are crucial for Europe?  Questions to be addressed include:  How will the U.S. election impact the current transatlantic alliance?  The U.S. is the EU’s largest trade and investment partner. How will the U.S. incoming president’s economic stance impact Europe’s industrial base?  What will a new administration mean for Europe and global challenges such as trade, China, and security?  How can the EU best prepare for the next U.S. administration?  Three weeks before American citizens head to the polls, this event, co-organized by AmCham EU & POLITICO, brings perspectives across both sides of the Pond for a candid debate on the U.S. election’s ramifications for Europe. description: “It is a major effort we’re asking for, I’m aware of that, but it’s a necessary and temporary one,” Armand said. Fabrice Le-Saché, vice-president of France's powerful MEDEF business lobby, agreed that companies could contribute to France’s budget efforts but said he’s concerned that the tax hikes may end up becoming permanent, as such temporary measures sometimes do.
text: “These tax measures will not hit the lower incomes, the middle classes and those who work,” Saint-Martin told reporters. “It is a path that rules out any tax bullying or austerity cure. There’s no ambiguity about that. We’re not going to put public finances back on track by destroying growth.”  Among the proposals were higher taxes on the wealthiest 0.3 percent of French taxpayers. Saint-Martin said that measure will only impact around 65,000 households.  But even those who aren’t hit directly by the new special taxes may feel the impact of the budget squeeze.  The government is, for instance, proposing to slash €3.8 billion in healthcare spending and to delay inflation adjustments for pensions until July. New taxes on plane tickets and polluting vehicles will likely be passed on to consumers as well.  Despite the rosy prediction from the government, France’s High Council for Public Finances, an independent watchdog, warned that the strategy unveiled on Thursday was “fragile” and overly optimistic.  Business are worried that the government’s aggressive plans could stymie growth as well, especially a proposed two-year corporate tax hike that will affect around 440 corporations with turnovers above €1 billion. Barnier’s government is also postponing several planned tax reductions for companies, raising an existing tax on electricity production, and introducing a new tax on share buybacks.

text: Johnson faced criticism in 2021 when high-end designer Lulu Lytle’s refurbishment of the Downing Street flat cost at least £112,000. That far exceeded the £30,000 annual grant funded by the taxpayer.  Media reports at the time said the then-PM’s spouse Carrie Johnson had slammed the “John Lewis furniture nightmare” they inherited from Theresa May in 2019.  The funding of the refurb became particularly controversial when it was disclosed that Conservative donor David Brownlow helped cover the costs.  The Conservatives were fined £17,800 by the Electoral Commission for failing to properly declare donations by Brownlow’s company Huntswood Associates used for the works. A government ethics probe cleared Johnson himself of any wrongdoing, but said he had acted “unwisely.”  When pressed on a reported total bill of £200,000 for the works, Johnson told LBC host Nick Ferrari that he didn’t recognize that figure. “It wasn’t as much as that,” he said.  Johnson would not be drawn on whether he liked the new wallpaper, which he denied was gold. “I’m not a great expert on wallpaper,” he added.  Johnson’s book, out this week, has already raised eyebrows in Westminster for its candid revelations, including details of the late Queen Elizabeth II‘s health in her final years; a suggestion Israel’s Benjamin Netanyahu bugged his bathroom; and the claim of a one-to-one pep talk with Prince Harry trying to dissuade the royal from leaving Britain.

text: "We consider UNIFIL's role as particularly crucial in light of the escalating situation in the region," the countries said in the statement, which was published on X by the Polish mission to the U.N.  The statement also urged "the parties of the conflict" to ensure the security and safety of the peacekeeping personnel "so that they can continue ... their work of mediation and support for peace and stability."  Spain, France and Italy had already slammed the attacks on UNIFIL as "unjustifiable." On Friday, U.S. President Joe Biden said he was "absolutely, positively" urging Israel to stop targeting U.N. peacekeepers.  UNIFIL said that its facilities have been "repeatedly hit" and that Israeli forces had "deliberately" fired shots at the mission's headquarters in the town of Naqoura.  Israeli forces asked UNIFIL to withdraw from some of its positions, but "there was a unanimous decision to stay" in the area, UNIFIL spokesperson Andrea Tenenti told AFP on Saturday.  On Sunday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu urged the U.N. peacekeepers in southern Lebanon to evacuate the region "immediately." In a video statement, Netanyahu told UNIFIL to move its personnel "out of harm's way," claiming that their presence in the region made them "hostages of Hezbollah."  Israeli tanks later Sunday destroyed the gate of a UNIFIL base in Ramyah and forcibly entered, leaving after 45 minutes, according to a statement by the U.N. mission. Israeli forces then fired several rounds 100 meters from the camp, causing skin irritation and gastrointestinal effects in 15 peacekeepers after smoke entered the base, it said.  UNIFIL was established as an interim force in 1978 to confirm Israel's withdrawal from Lebanon and help restore peace in the region. In 2006, when war broke out between Israel and Hezbollah, its mandate was expanded to monitor the cessation of hostilities and support the Lebanese army. The force counts more than 10,000 troops drawn from 50 countries, as well as about 800 civilian staff.

The United Kingdom accused Russia of deploying chemical weapons in its war on Ukraine, and is freezing the assets of agencies and enforcing travel bans on the individuals it says are responsible, the government said Tuesday.  The measures are targeted at the leadership of Russia’s radiological chemical and biological defense program, including its head Igor Kirillov, along with two labs run by Russia’s Defense Ministry.  In a statement, the U.K.’s Defense Secretary John Healey pointed to “horrific chemical attacks in Ukraine,” with the government claiming that such attacks mark a “flagrant violation” of the Chemical Weapons Convention, which dates back to the 1990s and compels signatory states to ban such warfare.

description: Pan-European television channel Euronews has fired its chief executive, Guillaume Dubois, with immediate effect. The Brussels-based media company's board of directors made the decision Friday afternoon, according to a letter Dubois sent to his staff, seen by POLITICO.
text: According to Dubois, the company underwent an “incredible transformation” under his leadership, necessitated by its “disastrous financial health.”  “Thanks to you, thanks to your daily commitment, the operating result for fiscal 2024 will be the best the company has seen in ten years,” Dubois wrote in the email.  One of Dubois' biggest decisions was to move the media company's headquarters to Brussels last year after being based in Lyon for decades. The move was painful as it meant cutting nearly 200 jobs in France.  “I’m not forgetting the efforts made by each and every one of you to achieve these results, and even more so the painful redundancy plan implemented in Lyon. As you know, I took this terrible decision in the name of the recovery of Euronews,” Dubois wrote.

description: Russia recruited an Irish agent to exploit Brexit tensions. He’s still sitting in Ireland’s parliament. Officials tell POLITICO Russia used a honeytrap to persuade the unidentified opposition lawmaker to push anti-NATO messages, and liaise with extremists in Northern Ireland.
text: When reporters asked Harris whether a Russian intelligence mole was operating within the parliament, the Irish prime minister said he couldn’t confirm the information, but added: “It shouldn’t come as any surprise to any of us.”  Harris said such efforts by Russian intelligence agents had increased in Ireland, as elsewhere, since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.  Back then, Ireland expelled four Russian diplomats accused of recruiting intelligence moles within Ireland’s political and business communities. Moscow retaliated by banning scores of Irish politicians from traveling to Russia, a move that drew mirth in Dublin.  “Russia seeks to distort public opinion, and is active in relation to that across the world. Ireland is not immune from that,” Harris said.  The officials told POLITICO the lawmaker had been recruited in 2019 as Russia sought to inflame Brexit-related tensions between Ireland and the U.K., particularly in the U.K. region of Northern Ireland. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because neither was authorized to discuss Ireland’s intelligence activity on the record.  Likewise, Harris said he couldn’t discuss the specifics of Irish intelligence on the lawmaker, who has been identified only as a current member of Ireland’s two-chamber parliament, the Oireachtas.

text: Guten Morgen, Berlin! Hier ist Gordon Repinski mit Ihrem Playbook aus dem Regierungsviertel! Gestern drehte sich alles um Miersch und Kühnert (auch bei meinen Kollegen war ich), heute dann um die Zukunft: Ich bin am Abend in Düsseldorf und spreche mit Hendrik Wüst und zahlreichen Entscheidern aus Nordrhein-Westfalen über die Lage der Nation. Optimismus garantiert. Und damit starten wir (trotzdem) aus Berlin!  Heute im Playbook: Radikale Ideen eines Grünen Finanzministers, Pläne zum Ampel-Ende, Orbán in Straßburg, Merz mahnt in der Fraktion, zwei Beförderungen in der Bundeswehr, eine neue MdB für Kreuzberg.  SEITE EINS  AMPEL-PHASE: In Berlin regiert die Ampel in Wut und Melancholie (SPD), Resignation (Grüne) und Ungläubigkeit (FDP) auf ihr sicheres Ende zu. Jede Kabinettssitzung könnte in diesem Herbst die letzte sein; wir grüßen in den Saal, heute ist es ja wieder so weit.  Zuweilen gibt es noch Vorschläge, wie man es besser machen könnte: von Danyal Bayaz etwa, dem Finanzminister aus Baden-Württemberg hier.  **(Anzeige) Eine Nachricht von INSM: Das Rentenpaket2 bringt weder Generationengerechtigkeit noch Fortschritt in Sachen Rente und Rentenbeiträgen. Warum das Rentenpaket2 so nicht beschlossen werden darf!**  Reform-Nostalgie: Bayaz fordert gegen den Abschwung eine große Investitionsagenda, bei der jede Partei „über ihren Schatten“ springe. „Wir brauchen eigentlich so etwas wie eine Agenda 2010“, sagt er mir im Playbook Podcast.  So spricht wirklich ein Grüner: Die wirtschaftlichen Schwierigkeiten seien nicht nur konjunkturelle, so Bayaz. Jetzt gehe es „wirklich um Business First“.  Zurück zum Verbrenner findet er naiv: „Wir brauchen mehr Freiräume für die Unternehmen (…) und wir müssen einfach wieder stärker bei neuen Technologien ansetzen.“  Von einer Kaufprämie hält er „nichts“: „Denn das haben wir beim letzten Mal bei der Abwrackprämie erlebt. Dann ist erst einmal kurzes Konjunkturfeuerwerk und dann kommt die Wachstumsstelle hinten raus.“  Im Playbook Podcast hören Sie das gesamte 200-Sekunden-Interview und in 15 Minuten das Wichtigste des Tages.  NEUWAHL-TERMIN? Angesichts des drohenden Ampel-Bruchs bereitet sich die Verwaltung schon mal vor. Nach der Sommerpause haben Bundespräsidialamt und die Bundestagsverwaltung ein Neuwahl-Szenario durchgespielt.  Ergebnis: Als Termin komme der 2. und 9. März infrage, berichten meine Kollegen Jürgen Klöckner und Hans von der Burchard. Aber: Der 2. März würde mitten in die Karnevalszeit fallen, einen Tag vor Rosenmontag. Dann besser der 9. März.  Die Annahme: Wenn die FDP Ende November (etwa im Haushaltskrach) aus der Koalition aussteigt, würde Scholz wahrscheinlich zur Vertrauensfrage gezwungen werden. Die würde (wie bei Schröder 2005) nicht unmittelbar kommen, sondern vermutlich erst in der Sitzungswoche Ende Dezember, kurz vor Weihnachten.  Ab dann liefe der Countdown von 21 Tagen für die Bundestagsauflösung durch Frank-Walter Steinmeier sowie anschließenden 60 Tagen bis zur spätmöglichsten Neuwahl. Der 9. März wäre das Limit – eine Woche nach der Hamburg-Wahl, bei der SPD und Grüne auf gutes Abschneiden und damit einen positiven Wahlkampfendspurt hoffen.  Eine weitere Bruchstelle ist der Soli: Am 12. November befasst sich das Bundesverfassungsgericht mit dem Thema. Die FDP hält den noch bestehenden Solidaritätszuschlag für verfassungswidrig, SPD und Grüne sind dafür. Argumentiert das Bundesverfassungsgericht gegen den Soli, hätte die FDP einen Vorwand für den Exit, der aus Sicht der Liberalen auch als Wahlkampfthema taugt.  KANZLERMAPPE  KABINETTSMITTWOCH: Um 11 Uhr treffen sich die Minister im Kanzleramt. Wir haben die Liste mit den Tops des Tages vorab.  Es geht unter anderem heute um die Zusammenarbeit mit Österreich bei der Luftsicherheit (Abkommen von 2022), bei einer Genehmigungspflicht für Soldaten, bei der Stärkung des deutschen Fondsmarktes und der Schaffung einer Digitalagentur für Gesundheit.  Erinnerungskultur: Nach der Kabinettssitzung fährt Olaf Scholz nach Leipzig, wo das 35. Jubiläum der Friedlichen Revolution besonders groß gefeiert wird. Um 14:30 Uhr spricht er über Demokratie beim Festakt im Leipziger Gewandhaus, Marianne Birthler hält ebenfalls eine Rede. Um 17 Uhr nimmt der Kanzler am Friedensgebet in der Nikolaikirche teil.  Lichtfest: Neben dem sächsischen Ministerpräsidenten Michael Kretschmer, dem Leipziger Oberbürgermeister Burkhard Jung und der ehemaligen DDR-Bürgerrechtlerin Elke Urban hält Scholz um 19 Uhr ein Grußwort auf dem Augustusplatz.  Selbst das BSW ist vertreten: Aus der Landtagsfraktion in Sachsen nehmen Jörg Scheibe, Doreen Voigt und Ronny Kupke an der Veranstaltung teil.  FRAKTIONSEBENE  UNIONS-KRACH ZU CHINA: Friedrich Merz kritisierte beim gestrigen Fraktionstreffen die unterschiedlichen Ampel-Haltungen zu EU-Zöllen auf Elektroautos aus China – nur um dann festzuhalten, dass er als Kanzler (ebenso wie Olaf Scholz) „gegen solche Zölle“ gestimmt hätte.  Pikanterweise stellt er sich damit diametral gegen seine eigenen Europapolitiker, berichtet Hans von der Burchard.  Klappt ja super mit der Absprache: Ebenfalls gestern verabschiedete die CDU/CSU-Fraktion im Europaparlament ein Positionspapier, das die EU-Maßnahmen ausdrücklich befürwortet. Es sei „richtig, dass die Kommission China die rote Karte zeigt“.  Angesprochen auf die Gegenmeinung des Parteivorsitzenden betonte der CDU-Europachef Daniel Caspary gegenüber Hans: Es gebe „eine massive Marktverzerrung, und da dürfen wir uns nicht von China erpressen lassen“. Bei Nicht-Handlung drohe „massiver Schaden“, der schwerer zu wiegen drohe als die negativen Auswirkungen der Zölle.  Im Konrad-Adenauer-Haus ist man dennoch nervös: Sollte die Autoindustrie ins Kreuzfeuer eines Handelskrieges geraten, würde das Merz’ Aufschwungpläne als nächster Kanzler gefährden. Gestern kündigte Peking erste Gegenmaßnahmen gegen Weinbrand-Importe wie französischen Cognac an. Aber auch deutsche Verbrennerautos geraten bereits ins Visier.  Ein Deal mit China könnte den Handelskrieg noch verhindern: „Aber es wird keine Verhandlungslösung geben, wenn man der Kommission vorher die Waffen aus der Hand schlägt“, kritisiert Caspary die Ablehnung durch Merz wie Scholz.  GEBURTSTAGSANRUF: Nachdem ein Treffen mit Ursula von der Leyen Ende September in Brüssel nicht zustande kam (Florian Kain berichtet hier), konnte Merz am Dienstag immerhin von einem Telefonat mit von der Leyen erzählen.  Leicht genervt: Merz mahnte (in Richtung der CSU-Kollegen vor allem), endlich die „schwachsinnige Koalitionsdiskussion“ rund um einen Ausschluss von schwarz-grün zu lassen. „Lasst uns um eine starke CDU kämpfen“, riet er.  Zu dem FAZ-Beitrag der Ost-Parteifreunde Voigt und Kretschmer, sagte er: „Was am letzten Freitag veröffentlicht worden ist, wäre von uns nie geschrieben worden.“ Es sei „das Äußerste, wozu wir bereit sind, dass es geschrieben wird“.  Ihr Playbook deutet: Das ist eine gelbe Karte.  Ihr Playbook deutet weiter: Das wird Kretschmer komplett wumpe sein und Voigt halbwegs.  Zu Kühnert hat Merz auch noch etwas gesagt: Dieser sei ein großes Talent, der zu schnell verschlissen worden sei. Nun gehe es mit Miersch klar „nach links“ mit der SPD.  PLENARSAALEBENE  REGIERUNGSBEFRAGUNG: Um 13 Uhr stehen Nancy Faeser und Volker Wissing heute im Kreuzverhör der Abgeordneten. Bei der Innenministerin dürfte es vor allem um illegale Migration, Terrorgefahr und das Sicherheitspaket gehen, das wegen Widerständen in ihrer SPD diese Sitzungswoche schon wieder nicht angenommen werden kann.  Wissing muss mit kritischen Fragen zu seiner Flugtaxi-Förderung, der Bahn-Krise sowie dem Streit ums Verbrenner-Aus und EU-Flottengrenzwerten rechnen.  EUROVISION  NEUER ÄRGER MIT VIKTOR ORBÁN: Heute stellt der ungarische Premier im Straßburger Europaparlament die Prioritäten seiner Ratspräsidentschaft vor. Einen Vorgeschmack auf die kontroverse Debatte lieferte Orbán bereits gestern, als er vor Journalisten von einem Migrations-„Blutbad“ sprach.  Nächste Woche droht Orbán-Streit auf dem EU-Gipfel: Es geht um den 50-Milliarden-Dollar-Kredit für die Ukraine, den Budapest blockiert. Die Mega-Finanzhilfe für Kyjiw, welche „Trump-sichere“ Unterstützung (zumindest für das nächste Jahr) garantieren soll, wird über die Zinsen auf eingefrorenes russisches Staatsbankvermögen finanziert.  Doch die USA weigern sich, ihrer geplanten 20-Milliarden-Beteiligung an der Absicherung des Kredits zuzustimmen, solange die Finanzierung wegen Orbán auf wackeligen Beinen steht: Denn derzeit kann er die Russland-Sanktionen – und damit die Beschlagnahmung der Zinsen – alle sechs Monate mit seinem Veto blockieren.  Washington fordert, dass die Verlängerung dieser sogenannten „Windfall Profits“ von sechs auf 36 Monate angehoben wird, um längerfristige Sicherheit zu schaffen. Doch auch hier blockiert Orbán. Beim Gipfel nächste Woche wollen die anderen EU-Regierungschefs ihn in die Mangel nehmen, um ihn doch noch umzustimmen.  Wie der Kredit auch noch ohne Orbán angenommen werden kann, und welche Risiken damit verbunden sind, erfahren Sie in unserem Europa-Briefing Brussels Decoded, das Sie hier kostenlos zur Probe abonnieren können. Außerdem spricht Hans zu dem Thema auch im Playbook Podcast.  KRITIK ZU ANLASSLOSER ÜBERWACHUNG: Vor dem Treffen der EU-Innenminister am Donnerstag meldet sich der Obmann des Digitalausschusses im Bundestag, Tobias Bacherle, mit einem Brandbrief an Mitglieder des EU-Parlaments und mehrerer nationaler Parlamente. Meinem Kollegen Jürgen Klöckner liegt das Schreiben vor.  Gegen Ungarn: Der Grüne-Politiker stellt sich hierbei gegen den von Ungarn vorgelegten Kompromiss zur CSA-Verordnung, in der es um die Bekämpfung des sexuellen Missbrauchs von Kindern geht.  Die Details und den Brief finden Sie ebenfalls in Brussels Decoded.  ZOLL-KONFLIKT: Paris und Berlin sind nicht mehr nur der Motor für die europäische Integration, sondern oft zerstritten. Das zeigen die E-Auto-Zölle ebenso wie das Mercosur-Abkommen.  Über den aktuellen Stand, die Folgen und Hintergründe diskutieren meine Kollegen Jürgen Klöckner, Oliver Noyan und Koen Verhelst am Donnerstag um 15 Uhr in einem POLITICO-Debrief. Hier können Sie sich noch anmelden, wir freuen uns auf Sie!  EMANZIPATION VOM TOXISCHEN EX: Daten zeigen, dass die meisten EU-Länder auch ohne russisches Gas gut auskommen würden, schreiben meine Kollegen Lucia Mackenzie und Gabriel Gavin.  BAND DES BUNDES  NÄCHSTER KASSEN-SCHOCK: Nach der Pflegeversicherung ist auch in der Gesetzlichen Krankenversicherung (GKV) die Finanzlage dramatischer als angenommen, berichtet Jürgen Klöckner.  Kommende Woche wird es ernst: Dann kommt der Schätzerkreis zusammen. Das Gremium, in dem unter anderem Kassen, das BMG und BMF sitzen, schätzt Einnahmen und Ausgaben der GKV. Daraus ergibt sich der nötige durchschnittliche Zusatzbeitrag 2025.  Die Hausnummer: In Kassenkreisen kursieren bereits deutlich höhere Zahlen als der vom GKV-Spitzenverband im Sommer prognostizierte Anstieg von 0,6 Prozentpunkten.  Laut Schätzung sei „eine Größenordnung von 0,7 Prozentpunkten realistisch“, sagte uns TK-Chef Jens Baas. An die GKV würden dann Beiträge in Höhe von 17 Prozent des Bruttolohns fließen – so viel wie nie. „Die Ausgaben steigen ungebremst und viel stärker als die Einnahmen.“ Er fordert einen höheren Steuerzuschuss und höhere Beiträge für Bürgergeldempfänger.  Der Chef einer anderen Krankenkasse hält sogar einen Anstieg um „0,8 oder sogar einen Prozentpunkt“ für nötig. „Gesundheitsminister Lauterbach darf die Lage nicht schönreden.“  Mit dem drohenden Beitragssprung in der Pflegeversicherung von geschätzten 0,3 Prozentpunkten wäre das kommende Wahljahr dann das teuerste in der Geschichte der Sozialversicherung. Die Beiträge für Kinderlose lägen bei knapp 43 Prozent.  112: Die desaströse Lage wird sich aus Sicht der Kassen durch die Krankenhausreform nur verschlimmern. Die Fraktionen planen 51 Änderungsanträge (hier). Ende kommender Woche soll die Reform dann im Bundestag beschlossen werden, kündigte Lauterbach gestern an.  Alleine im kommenden Jahr dürften die Kliniken die Kassen knapp acht Milliarden Euro mehr kosten, rechnete der GKV-Spitzenverband am Dienstag vor. 800 Millionen entfallen auf die Reform.  Keinesfalls dürfe die Reform „nur durch immer weiter steigende GKV-Beitragsmittel gezahlt werden“, warnte GKV-Verbandsvize Stefanie Stoff-Ahnis.  TAG DER ANGST IN HALLE: Frank-Walter Steinmeier ist zum Gedenken an den Terroranschlag auf die Synagoge in Halle. „Fünf Jahre, die so fern wirken und doch so nah sind. Vom Gedenken in Halle geht heute ein Zeichen der Menschlichkeit durch das Land“, sagt Josef Schuster vom Zentralrat der Juden Rixa Fürsen.  „Die Mahnung könnte nicht aktueller sein“, sagt Nancy Faeser im Vorfeld. „Wir werden weiter rechtsextreme Netzwerke zerschlagen, ihnen ihre Einnahmen entziehen und ihre Waffen wegnehmen.“  Fakt ist jedoch, dass sich die Sicherheitslage jüdischer Gemeinden seit dem Massaker der Hamas auf Israel am 7. Oktober erheblich verschlechtert hat, wie eine aktuelle Studie des Zentralrats der Juden zeigt.  SCHNELLERE ASYLVERFAHREN: Nancy Faeser ist mit den geplanten Verschärfungen des Gemeinsamen Europäischen Asylsystems (GEAS) an deutschen Flughäfen in Eile. Sie hat bei der EU-Kommission angefragt, ob diese früher umgesetzt werden können, berichtet die FAZ.  Die Grenzkontrollen will Olaf Scholz so lange wie möglich beibehalten. „Wir machen das so lange, wie das geht. Und das wird sehr lange sein“, sagte er in der Sendung „RTL Direkt spezial – Am Tisch mit Olaf Scholz“.  TRANSATLANTIK  JAHRHUNDERT-HURRIKAN NIMMT KURS AUF FLORIDA: Hurrikan Milton, ein Sturm von historischer Größe, soll laut dem US-Wetterdienst in der Nacht vom Mittwoch auf Donnerstag in der Region Tampa Bay in Florida auf Land treffen – einer Region mit mehr als 3 Millionen Einwohnern.  Meteorologen warnen vor katastrophalen Sturmfluten von bis zu 4,5 Metern Höhe, weniger als zwei Wochen nachdem bereits Hurrikan Helene in Florida wütete und 230 Menschenleben forderte.    Trump sieht darin ein Wahlkampfthema und verbreitet Desinformation. Er wirft Kamala Harris und Joe Biden fälschlicherweise vor, Gelder für die Katastrophenhilfe in Florida zweckzuentfremden und an Migranten weiterzuleiten.  DIPLOMATISCHE DEPESCHE  GESPRÄCH GEPLANT: Nach knapp zweimonatiger Funkstille und angesichts eines möglichen Vergeltungsschlags Israels gegen den Iran will Biden heute voraussichtlich mit dem israelischen Ministerpräsidenten Benjamin Netanjahu telefonieren, berichtet Axios.  INSIDE BASEBALL  ÄRGER MIT RYGLEWSKI: Zahlreiche Gesetze im Bereich Familie/Frauen sind aktuell in der Abstimmung zwischen dem Justiz- und dem Familienministerium. Darum gibt es nun Ärger: Denn das BMJ hat bei einigen der Vorhaben die Länder beteiligt, obwohl die Ressortabstimmung noch nicht eingeleitet war.  Montagsrunde: Am Montagnachmittag mahnte Staatsministerin Sarah Ryglewski, alle Häuser mögen sich bitte an die Geschäftsordnung halten – der Kommentar wurde klar in Richtung des BMJ gedeutet.  (NOCH) EINE GRÜNE WIRFT DAS HANDTUCH: Der Abgeordneten Canan Bayram sei es „immer weniger klar, wofür die Grünen eigentlich steht“. Das schreibt sie in einem Brief, in dem sie erklärt, nicht erneut für den Bundestag anzutreten. Sie bleibt jedoch im Amt bis zum Mandatsende.  Die innere Wahrheit: Ihr Kreisverband hatte sich längst gegen Bayram positioniert. Nun rechnen alle mit Katrin Schmidberger.  Ihr Kreuzberger Playbook sagt: Hauptsache keine Hinkelsteine auf die Bergmannstraße! Gruß geht raus an Monika Herrmann und Florian Schmidt!  FRÜHSCHICHT  6 Uhr – Nordkorea macht dicht: Das Land will sämtliche Straßen- und Eisenbahnverbindungen zu Südkorea unterbrechen. Zudem sollen die Gebiete auf nordkoreanischer Seite mit „starken Verteidigungsstrukturen“ befestigt werden, schreibt die staatliche Nachrichtenagentur KCNA.  2 Uhr – Ärger für Tiktok: 14 US-Generalstaatsanwälte verklagen die Videoplattform. Vorwurf: Der Service sei mit Absicht so gestaltet, dass Kinder und Jugendliche immer mehr Zeit dort verbringen wollten. Das schade ihrem Wohlbefinden. Tiktok weist die Vorwürfe zurück.  SPOTTED  „ES REICHT!“, schreibt Andreas Scheuer auf Instagram. Am Montag hieß es noch, er wird in Passau die Haushaltsführung übernehmen, doch gestern trat der gescheiterte Maut-Minister schon wieder zurück. Grund: „ein abgekartetes Spiel“ von Stadtrat und Medien, die sich „zum Steigbügelhalter der Bösartigkeit machen“ – und gegen ihn Kampagne fahren.  JOBWECHSEL  NEW GENERATION: Das Media-Management der Commerzbank hat Martin Härtel als Nachfolger von Andrea Tauber-Koch übernommen. Härtel war bereits als dualer Student vor 14 Jahren bei der Bank gestartet. Tauber-Koch war rund 15 Jahre für Media-Themen der Bank zuständig und geht nun in den Ruhe­stand.  STERN-BEFÖRDERUNGEN: In der Bundeswehr werden Johannes Werner Backus zum Generalstabsarzt und Jochen Helmut Deuer zum Generalmajor ernannt. Backus war bisher stellvertretender Inspekteur des Sanitätsdienstes im Kommando Sanitätsdienst. Deuer diente als Büroleiter des Generalinspekteurs.  AGENDA  — Die Regierungspressekonferenz findet um 13 Uhr statt.  — Frank-Walter Steinmeier empfängt um 11 Uhr den armenischen Präsidenten Wahagn Chatschaturjan.  — Informelle Tagung: Die Sozial- und Gesundheitsminister der EU-Länder treffen sich in Budapest.  — Eine Bundespressekonferenz findet um 14:15 Uhr mit Robert Habeck und seiner Abteilungsleiterin für Wirtschaftspolitik Elga Bartsch statt.  — Bundeskonferenz der Kommunalen Entwicklungspolitik: Svenja Schulze hält um 9:30 Uhr ein Grußwort bei der Preisverleihung des Wettbewerbs „Kommune bewegt Welt“ in Ingelheim am Rhein.  — Botschaftertreffen: Um 14:30 Uhr empfängt Cem Özdemir den spanischen Botschafter Pascual Navarro und die Botschaftsrätin für Landwirtschaft Lucia Garcia.  — Journalistische Gleichstellungsinitiative: Um 14 Uhr hält Lisa Paus ein Grußwort bei ProQuote Medien.  — 50. Paris – POLITICO, le média international leader sur la politique, les politiques publiques et le pouvoir, annonce aujourd’hui le lancement d’une nouvelle verticale en France dédiée à la politique numérique et à ses implications à Paris et au-delà. text: October 11  Paris – POLITICO, the global authority on politics, policy, and power, has today announced the launch of a new dedicated policy coverage area in France, focusing on the latest developments in technology legislation and their implications in Paris and beyond.  Launching on October 15, Pro Tech France joins Paris Playbook, Paris Influence, and Pro Energie & Climat as POLITICO continues to expand its operations across the country.  Leading this work in POLITICO’s Paris bureau are newly hired Tech Editor Tiphaine Saliou who joins after over a decade covering tech policy in the French capital. She will manage a new team of reporters including Océane Herrero, Emile Marzolf and Klara Durand, and work under the direction of Marion Solletty, Executive Editor, France.  Pro Tech France will join other dedicated verticals on the POLITICO Pro platform, the real-time policy intelligence service for professionals served by over 100 journalists.  Subscribers to Pro Tech France will receive a daily newsletter, Pro Tech Matin, every weekday morning at 07:30 CET. The newsletter will provide an essential rundown on what is expected to impact the tech industry and relevant legislation, from data privacy to AI regulation.  “The launch of Pro Tech France is another landmark moment for our editorial coverage in France,” said Marion Solletty. “This new team will deliver the type of impactful reporting POLITICO prides itself on, whilst also providing daily coverage and analysis on some of the most consequential topics facing our readers.”  Pro Tech France is the second offering dedicated to POLITICO Pro subscribers launched in the country this year, following the successful launch of Pro Energie & Climat France in April. Produced in French, both launches have taken place alongside the expansion of POLITICO’s newsroom in Paris to reaffirm the publication’s ambitions.  “Pro Tech France strengthens our coverage of one of the country’s most important sectors and joins the ranks of successful localised editions covering the tech industry in Brussels and London.” said Clémence Vatier, General Manager, France at POLITICO. “Our existing POLITICO Pro verticals have already proven to be invaluable to policy professionals in France, so we are delighted to expand our offering and support their work further.”  Readers can sign up for a five-week free trial of the Pro Tech Matin newsletter ahead of its launch on October 15.  More on the Pro Tech France team:  Tiphaine Saliou joins POLITICO from Contexte to serve as Tech Editor. With a deep focus on digital policy, Saliou has closely followed legislative developments in the digital sector, particularly cultural issues such as copyright law and anti-piracy measures. She will be managing the team and its output, including editing the flagship daily newsletter.  The newly formed Tech team will build on existing expertise with the internal hire of Océane Herrero, who joins after two years reporting on tech lobbying and regulation for Paris Influence. Herrero has broken multiple scoops for POLITICO during her time at the publication, most recently on the high-profile arrest of Telegram CEO Pavel Durov and will serve as Tech Reporter.  Emile Marzolf, previously with Acteurs publics, joins POLITICO as Tech Reporter. An expert on data protection, cloud and cybersecurity issues, Marzolf has a track record of scoops on the nexus between tech and government.  Klara Durand, previously with Le Figaro, also joins as Tech Reporter. Durand has extensively covered the ever-evolving world of content creators and influencers whilst also following the latest trends in digital media and social platforms, such as YouTube, Twitch, Instagram, and TikTok.  About POLITICO  POLITICO is the global authority on the intersection of politics, policy, and power. It is the most robust news operation and information service in the world specializing in politics and policy, which informs the most influential audience with insight, edge, and authority.  Founded in 2007, POLITICO has grown to a team of more than 1,100 journalists and media professionals across North America, and Europe. In October 2021, POLITICO was acquired by Axel Springer SE.

text: Good Tuesday morning. This is Dan Bloom.  DRIVING THE DAY  REAL FIGHT STARTS NOW: Keir Starmer hosts his Cabinet this morning with a new-look Downing Street operation around him and what allies are calling “Day One” (!) now safely out of the way. New chief of staff Morgan McSweeney will surely be in the room when the meeting of Starmer’s top team kicks off at 9.30 a.m., amid briefings to the newspapers about the “radical” changes he wants to make in No. 10. The now-departed Sue Gray will very much not be there, of course, and it all feels a bit first-day-at-a-new-school. Shame the TV cameras aren’t invited to capture it this time.  Make yourselves at home! Gray’s Cabinet allies can at least turn up feeling less fearful they’re also about to be ousted from their jobs. An excitable briefing by one of McSweeney’s allies to the Times on Sunday that he wanted a reshuffle after the Oct. 30 budget has been firmly batted down by Downing Street — a steer that gets written up by both the Times and Guardian. Still, Playbook is old enough to remember when Sue Gray was *definitely* staying in her job, so let’s see.  Take your pick: There are, of course, plenty of issues more serious than No. 10 staffing matters for the Cabinet to discuss today. Thursday’s workers’ rights bill, war in the Middle East or the increasingly narrow options for the budget, for starters (more on all below). As Starmer’s 100th day as PM looms this weekend, he could always try reeling off another Gordon Brown-style list of achievements. Or perhaps he’ll detect a teeny bit of frustration among colleagues about the endless negative headlines of late, and keep his powder dry. Who can say?  **A message from Xlinks: Xlinks’ Morocco-UK Power Project is essential for our energy transition, because the sun doesn’t always shine and the wind doesn’t always blow on our island. Xlinks will deliver 8% of the UK’s electricity needs with imported renewable energy. That’s why it has been recognised by DESNZ as a Project of National Significance. Find out more.**  Speaking of Labour bonhomie: Playbook hears No. 10’s “SpAd school” will meet at 6 p.m., with political advisers called in for one of their regular chats with Labour top brass. Colleagues widely expect McSweeney will attend, perhaps with his new deputies in tow. “I wouldn’t be surprised if they use it to drive home the political narrative,” says one aide.  SCOOP — ABOUT THAT POLITICAL NARRATIVE: Labour’s lead over the Tories has fallen to just *1* point, according to a More in Common poll shared with Playbook. One point! The survey of 2,023 British adults has Labour on 29 percent, the Conservatives on 28, Reform UK on 19, the Lib Dems on 11 and Greens on 7. That historic landslide election victory suddenly feels an awfully long time ago.  Gulp: The poll was conducted over the past weekend, and so overlapped fairly neatly with the latest turmoil in No. 10. It’s the lowest Labour lead More in Common has recorded since it started doing voting intention polls last year, and is down from 4 points a fortnight ago. It is, of course, only one poll, and we’re nowhere near election time. But still … 1 point.  IT’S MORGAN’S WORLD NOW: “Radical change” is McSweeney’s answer to all this — at least when it comes to the inner workings of No. 10, officials have told the Guardian’s Pippa Crerar. She has been informed that “nothing” is “off the table” in the new-look No. 10 as “the day-to-day machinery of government doesn’t work properly … We’re expected to be running a powerful G7 economy yet sometimes it’s all quite small and analogue.”  Big target? Two people point out to my POLITICO colleagues Esther Webber and Sam Blewett that Starmer’s oft-cited “five missions” are (were?) a joint project of the PM and Sue Gray, and predict McSweeney may now reformulate them along politically punchier lines. Esther and Sam have an essential write-up of the No. 10 state of play here.  Early target: Crerar also hears McSweeney plans to finally sort out the issue of new SpAds’ pay. Playbook is told their probation periods are four months long, which means if the issue drags on much longer, many SpAds would face the indignity of working out their entire probation before they are even offered a long-term contract.  The new Dominic Cummings: Crerar is also told that McSweeney wants to take a more “data-led” approach to government. “This sounds like Dom,” one weary former No. 10 SpAd texts in.  SUE FIGHTBACK: But all is not sweetness and light under the glorious new leader. The Times splashes on an intriguing story by Oliver Wright and Steven Swinford, sourced to “senior government figures” who say No. 10 has wider problems that Gray’s exit won’t solve. One tells the pair Gray was the victim of “out of control special advisers.” Another says it prompted at least one senior woman not to apply for the job of Cabinet secretary.  Thinking the same: Labour peer and former Gordon Brown aide Stewart Wood is blunt, telling Esther and Sam for their piece: “It’s a welcome thing to have a political spine in the top team in a way that clearly wasn’t there in the first two or three months.” But a long-serving MP echoes the warnings that this whole thing is a problem for the PM personally: “Starmer lacks people skills, and has surrounded himself with people with the same problem.” Ouch.  Grid ire: An ally of Gray told the Times she didn’t run the No. 10 grid, despite extremely widespread briefings to the contrary.  Bottleneck to the last: Gray may soon fade from public consciousness, but not before hacks are given details of her new job (non-job?) as “envoy” to the nations and regions. The Cabinet Office still hadn’t published anything last night despite No. 10 saying the information would arrive “shortly.” Even when the description does appear — and you’d think No. 10 would want to get it out the way before PMQs — your author hears it is unlikely to detail a salary.  SCOOP — NOW WE’RE IN BUSINESS: A meeting over in the Cabinet Office this afternoon may well have more free-flowing debate than the Cabinet. Ministers Angela Rayner and Jonathan Reynolds will show union and business leaders the shape of Labour’s long-negotiated workers’ rights plan, Playbook hears, in the last big “tripartite” summit before it is unveiled on Thursday. The pair are due to brief general secretaries and union officials on the Employment Rights Bill, along with leaders of the “big five” industry groups including the Federation of Small Businesses, from about 4.30 p.m.  Laying the ground: Reynolds (watched by Rayner) gave MPs some basic detail in last night’s Parliamentary Labour Party meeting, including that some things won’t be either in the bill or in immediate consultations — such as creating a new single status of worker. As your Playbook author wrote on Friday, the government is set to create Day One rights to sick pay, make it easier to request a four-day “compressed” week and allow full rights to claim unfair dismissal after six months. But many details are set to go into consultations, which one official says are likely to be long.  As for Thursday itself … It’s only the bill’s first reading, so there’s no debate and no ministerial statement planned either, with Reynolds and Rayner planning a visit in northern England. The bill will be paired with a document spelling out the consultations.  WHAT THE GOVERNMENT WANTS TO TALK ABOUT: A “bus manufacturing expert panel” and a £500 million investment by Go Ahead into 1,200 zero-emission buses. Transport Secretary Louise Haigh is on the morning round to discuss a “new era of green growth.”  Er, about that growth: Haigh will doubtless be grilled on her announcement last night that a decision on the £9 billion Lower Thames Crossing — of 359,866-page planning application fame — has been delayed by a further seven and a half months, to take into account “any decisions made as part of the spending review.” A test for Chancellor Rachel Reeves’ push for growth.  Tightrope’s tight: Reeves receives her last “pre-measures” forecast from the Office for Budget Responsibility today, and the Guardian’s Richard Partington reckons Wednesday is the deadline for her to decide if she’s going to tweak Britain’s fiscal rules — which pretty much everyone thinks will happen. The Labour-friendly IPPR think tank reckons it could free up £57 billion of “headroom,” while IFS economists will give their view at the Lords Economic Affairs Committee from 3 p.m.  Tighter: The FT splashes on a steady rise in Britain’s long-term borrowing costs.  IN THE MIDDLE EAST: Fighting intensified on all sides on Monday’s first anniversary of Hamas’ Oct. 7 attacks on Israel. Foreign Secretary David Lammy told Channel 4 News he’ll be “back in the region this week, urging restraint.” Though Playbook is told it’s not Israel, Lebanon or (obv) Iran.  Things can only get worse: The i splashes on Starmer refusing to rule out U.K. military involvement — or a vote by MPs on such involvement — if Israel attacks Iran in response to Iran’s missile attack on Israel last week, from his Commons statement on Monday.  PLANET TORY  TUGENDSPLAT: Tory MPs will cut four leadership candidates to three this afternoon — and judging by their mood in the bars last night, the general vibe remains that former Security Minister Tom Tugendhat is heading for the exit first. Won’t somebody think of the merch?  That said … While Tugendhat’s team admit it’s an “uphill struggle,” they insist MPs and hacks are wrong to write off their man and they’re confident there is a way through for him today. If the SW1 commentariat ends up with proper egg on its face, we’ll soon know. A hustings for MPs is due at 11 a.m., voting starts at 1.30 p.m. and results are at 3.30 p.m.  Squeeze that TT-branded stress ball: Hacks will breathe a sigh of relief to hear that none of the four are doing media this morning. Instead, it’s one last stint pestering colleagues for support over breakfasts, lunches, dinners, coffees, phone calls, texts, in offices and in the tearoom. Thoughts and prayers.  Numbers game: All eyes will be on how close the candidates get to the golden threshold of 40 MPs, needed to pass into the final two on Wednesday. A total of 119 votes are up for grabs, as Leader Rishi Sunak and 1922 committee Chair Bob Blackman will sit the election out.  Reminder: Last time Robert Jenrick got 33 votes … Kemi Badenoch 28 … and James Cleverly and Tom Tugendhat 21 each.  Striding ahead: Cleverly last night won the backing of Sunak/Gove ally Mel Stride — who surely will be rewarded with the shadow chancellor job he covets if Cleverly wins. But Tories across the board tell Playbook Stride’s 16 supporters won’t move in a bloc, and the i’s Kitty Donaldson heard the same last week. So nothing is guaranteed.  NEVER TOO LATE FOR A YELLOW CARD: The war of words between backers of Tugendhat and Cleverly over the government’s handover of the Chagos Islands’ sovereignty appears to be getting worse. Tugendhat’s team are hoping his speech in Monday’s debate, in which he said Foreign Secretary David Lammy was trying to sell magic beans, will win over MPs who are doubtful that Cleverly did enough to stop it.  More harsh words: One backer of a rival campaign tells Playbook: “It’s making people look at James in a different light — it shows he’s not the all-conquering hero.” Rivals excitedly shared Charles Moore’s acidic Telegraph article that says Cleverly “did not always master his ministerial subjects.” But a Cleverly campaign figure says in the 15 months he was foreign secretary he didn’t come close to a handover: “There is no point pretending this is anything other than Labour’s deal.”  But but but … Telegraph U.S. Editor Tony Diver has a story that complicates the narrative. He reckons senior U.S. officials pushed the U.K. toward the deal out of fear that, without one, Mauritius could seek a binding ruling at the International Court of Justice — which would shutter the islands’ U.K.-U.S. air base. Diver also hears the treaty will contain some kind of protection against Chinese influence in the islands unless Britain and the U.S. agree.  AS FOR CLEVERLY: His team is still hopeful his good week will get him through, without having to tack left to pick up enough votes. They are pointing to More in Common research that claims he would do best in a head-to-head against Keir Starmer.  Fool me twice: The Mirror’s Dave Burke has managed to root out a *second* sports freebie to which Cleverly took his wife … was photographed with her in the stands … and ministerial hospitality records then said he didn’t bring any family.  IN THE JENRICK CAMP: The right-winger’s team believes he will have around 35 MPs today, and will pick up a “good chunk” of Tugendhat’s support if he is knocked out. She needs to be up to 36 or 37 today to make it … Kemi’s challenge is she’s nobody’s second place.”  Her team say … that she has the most councilors, the most peers and the most former MPs declared in her favor. They argue she came out top in More in Common focus groups where participants watched the quad’s conference speeches in full, and contrast her talking about “ideas and the size of the state” to her rivals’ focuses. In it, Johnson calls Labour’s policy of standing with Israel but banning some arms sales “completely incoherent and shocking.”  World’s shortest memory: Johnson also tells LBC: “I have no donors paying for my suits. Or spectacles. Who pays for your spectacles? You pay for your spectacles, don’t you? It’s unbelievable … that looks greedy.” This is the same Boris Johnson who had donors pay for his wedding, his family’s accommodation and a furnished office space valued at £7,100 a month. description: PARIS — French pharmaceutical giant Sanofi said on Friday that it was in talks to sell a majority stake of its subsidiary that produces over-the-counter drugs to an American private equity firm CD&R for €15 billion.
text: In the past, the French government has not hesitated to use those powers to block takeovers it viewed as dangerous, ranging from supermarkets to nuclear suppliers. A group of 62 centrist and conservative lawmakers sent Armand a letter on Friday calling upon the government to intervene.  "The French government will mobilize all the tools at its disposal, including those for controlling foreign investment in France," Economy Minister Antoine Armand and junior Industry Minister Marc Ferracci said in a statement.  The ministers, however, said that the buyer was "serious." They promised that any deal would not have an impact on the production and the supply of paracetamol and other essential medicines in France.  French lawmakers were quick to slam the possibility of a corporate takeover that would see the country's omnipresent yellow boxes of Doliprane, the brand name of Sanofi's paracetamol, in American hands. | Amaury Cornu/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images  Despite those assurances, French lawmakers were quick to slam the possibility of a corporate takeover that would see the country's omnipresent yellow boxes of Doliprane, the brand name of Sanofi's paracetamol, in American hands — especially given the hundreds of millions of euros the company has received in state aid. French President Emmanuel Macron last month inaugurated a new Sanofi vaccine factory which he said benefitted from €240 million of French state aid.  The head of the far-right National Rally, Jordan Bardella, said it would be "incomprehensible for the state to let this happen." Left-wing lawmaker Eric Coquerel, who chairs the National Assembly finance committee, said that "it is unthinkable to give up our sovereignty over the production of this type of medicine" and stressed that Sanofi was "flush with public money."  Lawmakers from Macron's centrist camp also castigated the possible deal.  France has in recent years provided generous subsidies to drugmakers in a bid reshore domestic medicine production, especially paracetamol, after critical shortages emerged during the coronavirus pandemic due to a global reliance on overseas suppliers. In parallel, the European Commission is working on a Critical Medicines Act to reduce Europe’s reliance on other countries for drugs.

description: Sweden is trying to crack down on kids being recruited into crime on online platforms — and it wants the European Union to step in. The Scandinavian country has in the past few years been rocked by a juvenile gang crime wave, described in 2020 as a “second pandemic” by then-opposition leader and current Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.. The Swedish government is now sounding the alarm at ...
text: This is a “particularly concerning aspect” of the gangs’ activities, the country said in a note that it presented to EU home affairs ministers Thursday, seen by POLITICO.  Alongside partners from the other Nordic countries, the Swedish government raised the issue with Meta, Google, Snap and TikTok in a meeting last month. But now the country wants the EU to step in, too.  Sweden asked ministers on Thursday whether they agreed that one of the bloc’s landmark digital laws would apply to online criminal recruitment.  The Scandinavian country has in the past few years been rocked by a juvenile gang crime wave. | Adam Ihse/TT News Agency/AFP via Getty Images  The Digital Services Act (DSA), passed last year, is an attempt by the EU to force companies to clean up their online platforms. The biggest players — including Facebook, Snap, YouTube and TikTok — have a special designation obligating them to meet more stringent requirements under the DSA. One of the big platforms’ responsibilities is tackling “systemic” risks resulting from the way their services are built.  "In our view, online recruitment constitutes 'systemic risks … stemming from the design or functioning of their service and its related systems, including algorithmic systems,'" Sweden said in its note.  Companies that fail to comply with the DSA face sweeping fines of up to 6 percent of their global annual revenue.

description: After three months of a European Council's presidency that has turned into a debacle, what can the EU do now with Orbán? Radio Schuman asks Daniel Hegedüs, Regional Director for Central Europe ...
text: ADVERTISEMENT  Halfway through its six-month rotating presidency, rather than playing the honest broker, Budapest has blocked many files, including the ones on aid to Ukraine.  It further blocked a statement denouncing Moscow's media ban, and it voted against the EU’s plan to impose tariffs on electric vehicles. It's unclear what exactly broke the camel's back, but one thing is certain: the EU has lost its patience with Hungary.  Yet on Tuesday, at a press conference ahead of this speech in Parliament, Orbán played the now-traditional martyr card at a press conference before his big speech in front of all MEPs, arguing that he's not the problem — it is Brussels that needs to change its strategy on Ukraine, migration and competitiveness.  So, what can the EU do now with Hungary? We ask Daniel Hegedüs, the German Marshall Fund's regional director for Central Europe.  Coming up on Wednesday’s EU agenda, Radio Schuman will dive into the latest developments on the G7's proposed €45 billion loan to Ukraine — will we see further progress?  Over in Strasbourg, MEPs are set for a lively debate on several key issues, including a G20 proposal to tax the world’s wealthiest individuals, strengthening the security of Europe’s external borders, and ensuring decent and affordable housing for all citizens.  And lastly, have you ever wondered if MEPs get to skip the airport lines? Or what benefits do they have? Short answer: the European Parliament does not issue passports with diplomatic status for MEPs, but they can have a "laisser-passez" travel document when going on parliamentary business.  Read the full story from James Thomas on euronews.com  Radio Schuman is hosted and produced by Maïa de la Baume, with journalist and production assistant Paula Soler, audio editing by Zacharia Vigneron and music by Alexandre Jas.

description: European states have unanimously endorsed Israel’s right to self-defence following Hamas’ 7 October attacks, but concerns that Western-donated weapons could be contributing to war crimes and ...
text: ADVERTISEMENT  Calls for an arms embargo on Israel have stepped up, 12 months after the war in Gaza broke out and as Israel widens its offensive against Iran-backed militants in the region.  Over the weekend, France’s President Emmanuel Macron accused governments who call for a ceasefire in Gaza while continuing to supply Israeli forces with lethal weapons of incoherence, drawing a stern rebuke from Israeli Premier Benjamin Netanyahu.  European states have unanimously endorsed Israel’s right to self-defence following Hamas’ 7 October attacks, but concerns that Western-donated weapons could be contributing to war crimes and civilian deaths in the besieged Gaza Strip have fuelled calls for an arms embargo.  High-stakes legal cases, such as South Africa’s genocide case against Israel before the UN’s top court, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), have upped the pressure on governments to avoid complicity in war crimes against civilians in Gaza.  European states are also party to the Arms Trade Treaty, which forbids them from authorising the transfer of arms that could be used in “attacks directed against civilian objects”.  Between 2019 and 2023, the US accounted for over two-thirds (69%) of all arms sold to Israel from abroad, while Germany was the second biggest supplier at 30%, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.  Any other European deliveries of lethal weapons and military equipment have accounted for less than 1% of all purchases, of which Italy has accounted for 0.9%.  It means political commitment to backing Israel militarily in Washington, and to a lesser extent in Berlin, have been critical in sustaining Israel’s capacity to wage what has been described as one of the deadliest and most destructive military campaigns in history.  The EuroVerify team breaks down how European countries have responded to calls for an arms embargo.  Germany  Germany’s support for Israel is considered part of its “reason of state”, or Staatsräson, due to its role in the Holocaust. It means that Berlin is by far the biggest European supplier of arms to the Jewish state.  Yet, data shows that Germany has slammed the brakes on arms sales to Israel since the start of this year, although Berlin has categorically denied changing its policy.  Data provided by the German Economy Ministry — which approves export licences —shows that while it approved €326.5 million in arms to Israel in 2023, it approved just €14.5 million between January and mid-August 2024.  It comes amid mounting legal and political pressure on the country to ensure it is not complicit in potential breaches of international law in the Gaza Strip. In a high-profile case brought by Nicaragua before the ICJ, Germany has been accused of breaching the UN genocide convention by sending arms to Israel.  France  Macron assured over the weekend that France had ceased transferring arms to Israel.  That claim is backed by data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, which shows no French exports of arms to Israel since 1998.  ADVERTISEMENT  However, France has continued to supply parts to Israel that could be used in its own domestic production of arms.  Israel has reportedly ramped up domestic production to reduce dependencies on foreign suppliers, as countries delay or threaten to cease arms transfers to the country.  French investigative media Disclose revealed in June that Paris had supplied equipment for the production of Israeli drones used in the offensive on Gaza.  Spain  The Spanish government says it has suspended its arms sales to Israel since 7 October, when the offensive in Gaza began.  ADVERTISEMENT  In May, Madrid went further by denying port of call to ships carrying arms to Israel, following pressure from left-wing partners in Pedro Sánchez’s coalition government.  However, Spanish investigative journalists citing figures obtained from a government portal say munition in the value of €987,000 was exported from Spain to Israel in November 2023, as part of an export licence approved before the 7 October attacks.  Italy  Italy, considered the third biggest foreign supplier of arms to Israel after the US and Germany, assured in the wake of the 7 October attacks that it would cease to supply arms to Israel.  But in March this year, the Italian Defence Ministry acknowledged orders signed before 7 October had been delivered during the war, despite Italian law banning the export of lethal weapons to countries at war.  ADVERTISEMENT  Belgium  Arms exports are handled at the regional level in Belgium, and the French-speaking Wallonia region says it has suspended licences for ammunition since the war broke out.  Belgium’s development minister Caroline Gennez has also called for an EU-wide arms embargo on Israel.  The United Kingdom  In September, the recently-elected Labour-led government of Prime Minister Keir Starmer announced it had suspended 30 of 350 arms export licenses to Israel after it found a “clear risk certain military exports to Israel might be used in violations of International Humanitarian Law”.  According to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, the UK still supplies components to Israel used in F-35 combat aircraft used to target the Gaza Strip.

description: The Entry/Exit System is a comprehensive reform to modernise checks at the EU's external borders and promote information-sharing.
text: ADVERTISEMENT  The European Commission has decided to delay the introduction of the Entry/Exit System (EES), the bloc's automated registry for short-stay travellers that was expected to come into force on 10 November.  The announcement was made by Ylva Johansson, the Commissioner for Home Affairs, at the end of a meeting of EU interior ministers on Thursday where the issue was discussed.  "10th of November is no longer on the table," Johansson told reporters, noting that Germany, France and the Netherlands had declared their unreadiness.  "I hope we can start as soon as possible but there's no new timeline so far. This also depends on the legal assessment that we will do and we're working on it right now."  Johannson spoke of "some concerns when it comes to the resilience of the system."  As an alternative, she said, the EU could introduce the EES in a phased-in manner "with a little step by step going into the system, not a Big Bang of all border crossing points at the same time."  However, that approach is not foreseen under the current regulation and "targeted amendments" to the legal text would be required to make it happen.  At any rate, she stressed, the gradual introduction would not start on 10 November.  What is the Entry/Exit System?  The EES is a comprehensive reform that dates back to 2016 and had been repeatedly delayed. Its main purpose is to modernise checks at the EU's external borders and replace the traditional physical stamping of passports.  It will apply to non-EU citizens who come to the bloc for visits, holidays or business trips and stay for a total duration of up to 90 days within a 180-day period.  Once the system goes live, visitors will have to provide their passports on arrival, alongside having a photo of their face taken and their fingerprints scanned electronically.  All entries and exits from the passport-free Schengen Area will be recorded.  The collection of biometric data and the sharing of information in real time are meant to help authorities crack down on those who overstay their short-term visas and commit identity fraud.  All member states, except Cyprus and Ireland, and four Schengen-associate countries – Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland – will take part in the scheme.  Passports in Cyprus and Ireland will continue to be stamped manually.

description: Days after news broke of the earthquake in Iran's Semnan province, speculation has continued on social media that the tremors were caused by Tehran's first nuclear test.
text: By Ali Shamdanihagh  ADVERTISEMENT  At 10:45 pm on Saturday, the University of Tehran's seismography centre announced that a 4.4-magnitude earthquake had shaken the city of Aradan in Iran's Semnan province, with tremors also felt in parts of eastern Tehran.  The epicentre of the earthquake, which occurred 12km below ground, were recorded as 35.42° north and 52.78° east.  Hours after the news broke, social media users began speculating that the Tehran regime had attempted to conduct its first underground nuclear test, presumably as a deterrent measure against Israeli attacks on its territory.  These speculations came as Islamic Republic officials and Revolutionary Guard commanders repeatedly threaten that if economic, political and military pressures on the country intensify, Tehran will alter its military defence doctrine — a change that would require amending the Iranian leader's fatwa on the illegality of nuclear weapons.  Nevertheless, the NorNews news website, which operates informally as the Islamic Republic's National Security Council main information outlet, dismissed the nuclear speculation as “rumours” and once again stressed that nuclear testing contradicts Iran's nuclear and defence doctrine.  However, the notion that Iran would never conduct such a test without announcing a change in policy does not necessarily stand up to scrutiny.  Does Iran have any secret testing sites?  In 2019, the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington-based think tank, released a report that Iran had begun a program to build underground nuclear testing sites, known as the “Field Project”.  The foundation has been sanctioned by Iran's Foreign Ministry for five years for “producing and disseminating lies, encouraging, consulting, lobbying, and negative propaganda campaign against the Islamic Republic with the aim of playing an effective role in imposing and intensifying economic sanctions”.  According to its 2019 report, its researchers "identified the likely location (in an area southeast of Semnan) where underground non-nuclear explosives tests were conducted in 2003 as part of developing seismic methods of measuring the yield of an underground nuclear explosive."  This raises the prospect that the earthquake reported in Semnan could be connected to Tehran's first nuclear test.  While Iran has previously acknowledged the existence of the "Imam Khomeini" space centre and missile headquarters southeast of Semnan, the site is more than 100 kilometres from the earthquake's epicentre.  However, some social media users continue to speculate that perhaps Iran has an undeclared underground nuclear facility in Semnan province, preferring to use it as a testing site instead of conducting them at a well-known facility such as Natanz.  Tehran has consistently failed to disclose its nuclear activities to the International Atomic Energy Agency. At the same time, Iran is an earthquake-prone country, and tremors like these are not uncommon or strange.
