text: Decoding transatlantic relations with Beijing.  By PHELIM KINE  with STUART LAU  Send tips here | Tweet @PhelimKine or @StuartKLau | Subscribe for free | View in your browser  Hi, China Watchers. Today we look at national security adviser Jake Sullivan’s latest statements on China, examine the impact of U.S. deportation flights of Chinese citizens who’ve violated U.S. immigration laws and examine a debate over Taiwan’s citizenship law. And we profile a novel that puts Taipei at the center of an “American coming of age novel.”  Let’s get to it. — Phelim.  Sullivan bullish on Biden China policies  The Biden administration’s efforts to push back against Chinese trade and economic policies that undermine U.S. competitiveness are starting to pay off — that’s the argument from national security adviser Jake Sullivan this week.  “Contrary to the predictions that the People’s Republic of China would overtake the U.S. in GDP either in this decade or next, since President Biden took office the United States has more than doubled our lead and last year the U.S. attracted more than five times more inbound investment than the next highest country,” Sullivan said at a Wednesday event at the Brookings Institution think tank in Washington.  Sullivan said Biden administration moves including targeted tariffs on Chinese imports and steering public and private investment into rebuilding the U.S. high tech industrial base contributed to those gains.  But there are questions about the potential long term utility of the administration’s strategy to outpace Beijing technologically and economically. China is managing to evade U.S. restrictions on high-end semiconductor exports. And Beijing is rallying BRICS countries — a grouping of emerging economies that along with China includes Brazil, Russia and India — to form a bloc of developing countries to compete with the economic partnerships that Biden is deepening with U.S. allies and partners.  Sullivan didn’t mention Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris in his comments. But their timing— just 13 days prior to the U.S. presidential election in which the economy is front-and-center — is a tacit nod to Harris’ role in an administration claiming to have knocked back Beijing while helping rebuild the U.S. industrial base.  Sullivan also hinted that GOP presidential candidate Donald Trump’s plans for steep across-board tariff increases — including a proposed 60 percent tariff on Chinese imports — would be counterproductive. Biden’s application of tariffs has been “smart and strategic…[and] had a core logic, while “indiscriminate, broad based tariffs will harm workers and businesses, both in the United States and our partners,” Sullivan said.  The specter of Beijing’s growing economic might and the risk of “a second China shock” dominated Sullivan’s remarks, which reiterated many of the dangers he outlined in a 2023 speech he gave on renewing American economic leadership.  Diversification of supply chains is essential “so that no country, particularly China, can hold us hostage,” Sullivan said. Ensuring reliable access to critical minerals is necessary to prevent the U.S. from becoming “increasingly dependent on a country that has demonstrated its willingness to weaponize such dependencies,” he added. Sullivan also warned of Chinese-connected vehicles getting “daily software updates” and “sending reams of information back” to China as a growing national security risk.  There are also domestic political obstacles to effectively competing with China that Sullivan blamed on the U.S. Congress. “Congress still hasn’t appropriated the ‘science’ part of CHIPS and Science, even while the PRC is increasing its science and technology budget by 10 percent year on year,” Sullivan said.  And he called for congressional renewal next year of policy tools including the International Development Finance Corp. and the African Growth and Opportunity Act, arguing that they are essential for countering China’s growing influence among developing countries. Congressional authorization for both of those programs expires in Sept. 2025.  Those renewals may get a cold shoulder if the GOP retains control of the House in the next Congress. House Republicans — led by firebrand Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.) —have campaigned to cut funding for what she has described as “wasteful” international aid programs.  Mayorkas wrangles deportation flights of Chinese citizens  Beijing has lifted its years-long refusal of repatriation flights of Chinese citizens who have violated their U.S. visa status — but don’t call it a breakthrough yet.  A flight of Chinese deportees left the U.S. last week, the second such removal of visa violators that DHS has wrangled permission from Beijing to return since 2018. Those flights follow months of diplomatic arm-twisting by Department of Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas. But neither DHS nor the Chinese government has signaled that those two flights are the start of a long term campaign to remove the huge numbers of Chinese citizens in the U.S. eligible for deportation.  Drop in the bucket. DHS estimated that Beijing was refusing to accept the return of “approximately 40,000 PRC nationals” in 2021. DHS declined to comment on specific steps it’s taking to continue such deportations and reduce the number of Chinese nationals currently in immigration detention.  Migrant surge. The number of Chinese citizens illegally entering the U.S. has soared in the past two years. U.S. authorities picked up more than 37,000 Chinese citizens who illegally crossed the Mexican border into the U.S. in 2023. That’s a near-tenfold increase in the number of such detentions in 2022.  Skeptics abound. That makes those two flights “a pretty meaningless token… more electioneering publicity stunt than real deterrence,” said Todd Bensman, former manager of counterterrorism intelligence at the Texas Department of Public Security and now a senior fellow at Washington-based nonprofit Center for Immigration Studies. GOP lawmakers are also dubious. “Why has there not been more aggressive diplomacy to pressure China…to accept more repatriation flights?” said Rep. Mark Green (R-Tenn.), chair of the House Homeland Security Committee.  Resource poor. Green’s counterpart on the other side of the aisle says DHS lacks the cash to pay for high numbers of deportation flights. The agency “needs appropriate resources to ensure all migrants are properly vetted, processed, and removed consistent with the outcome of their cases,” said Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.), ranking member of the House Homeland Security Committee.  Denial reflex. Still, it does mark a departure from Beijing’s long history of refusing the return of Chinese citizens who’ve violated U.S. immigration law. “We tried to do that in the Bush administration — turns out the Chinese don’t want criminals back, they only wanted political dissidents,” said Paul Rosenzweig, former DHS deputy assistant secretary for policy under President George W. Bush. Chinese authorities went so far as to declare prospective deportees’ Chinese passports “fake” to justify denying their return, Rosenzweig said.  The Chinese embassy in Washington declined to comment.  Felons at large. DHS argued in 2021 that China’s refusal to assist such deportations constituted a national security threat. Lack of space in immigration detention facilities compels U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement “to release hundreds of PRC nationals, many with convictions for violent crimes, into American communities, jeopardizing public safety.”  GOP lawmakers share that threat assessment. The House Subcommittee on Oversight, Investigations, and Accountability held a hearing entitled, “Security Risk: The Unprecedented Surge in Chinese Illegal Immigration” in May. Their Democratic committee colleagues dubbed the hearing “Another Republican border ‘hearing’ with invasion rhetoric and fear mongering.”  Dreamers, not schemers. The Democrats’ doubts may be justified. The vast majority of unauthorized Chinese migrants “are here to work and pursue an ‘American dream’ they don’t see as possible in China — Chinese spies who are here have better, less risky ways to enter than crossing the border illegally and risking attention from DHS,” argued Meredith Oyen, an associate professor of history at the University of Maryland Baltimore County and an expert on the role of migrants in the history of U.S.-China relations.  TRANSLATING WASHINGTON  — DEFENSE INTELLIGENCE WARNS ON CHINA NUKES: Beijing is undertaking a massive increase in its nuclear arsenal that will double its current number of warheads to more than 1,000 by 2030, the Defense Intelligence Agency said in a report Wednesday. That’s “the most rapid expansion and ambitious modernization of its nuclear forces in history—almost certainly driven by an aim for enduring strategic competition with the U.S.,” according to the report. U.S. efforts to coax Beijing into nonproliferation talks hit a brick wall in July after China suspended negotiations to protest U.S. arms sales to Taiwan.  — VATICAN’S BEIJING DEAL DRAWS U.S. FIRE: The chair of the U.S. Commission on International Religious Freedom has criticized the Vatican’s decision this week to extend a four-year agreement with the Chinese government allowing joint approval of new bishops in China’s state-controlled Catholic Church. Chinese authorities “have continued to detain and forcibly disappear underground Catholic clergy who refuse to join the state-controlled Chinese Catholic Patriotic Association,” said Stephen Schneck, chair of the federal government body. The agreement came days after Washington-based think tank Hudson Institute published a report entitled “Ten Persecuted Catholic Bishops in China.”  The deal marks efforts to “seek continued improvement of ties,” between the Vatican and Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said on X Tuesday. Beijing has long aimed to prod the Holy See to normalize diplomatic ties —a move that would require the Vatican to drop its existing recognition of Taiwan. The Vatican’s embassy in Washington referred POLITICO to the Holy See’s press office, which didn’t respond to a request for comment.  — GOP LAWMAKERS BASH PRETORIA’S TAIWAN MOVES: The South African government’s efforts to compel Taiwan’s unofficial diplomatic outpost in Pretoria to relocate outside of the capital is taking Republican heat on Capitol Hill.  That decision is “a clear result of Chinese Communist Party coercion and brazen interference into the affairs of other nations,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Michael McCaul (R-Texas) said in an X post Tuesday. McCaul urged the South African government to reverse its “misguided action” and leave the Taiwan outpost in place. Rep. John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), chair of the House Select Committee on China, accused South Africa of siding with “authoritarian aggression.”  Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn) wants U.S. reprisals against Pretoria if it doesn’t do so. The Biden administration should “make it clear that there will be consequences if South Africa works with the Chinese Communist Party to bully Taiwan,” Blackburn said on X Monday. Top of Blackburn’s hit list — booting South Africa from eligibility under the U.S. African Growth and Opportunity Act, which allows duty-free import access for hundreds of products.  The South African embassy in Washington didn’t respond to a request for comment.  TRANSLATING EUROPE  EU’S NEXT FOREIGN POLICY CHIEF HARDENS STANCE ON CHINA: The EU’s future top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, dropped the first sign of a potentially harder line on China this week, singling out Beijing’s status as a systemic rival for the EU. (The EU officially recognizes China simultaneously as a partner — mostly on climate change — economic competitor and systemic rival.)  “My priority in engaging with China will be to safeguard the EU’s geopolitical and economic security,” Kallas said Wednesday in her written statement to the European Parliament preparing for her confirmation hearing. “The most pressing challenges here are China’s support for Russia as well as structural imbalances between the EU and China that result from non-market policies and practices, which create unfair competition and an unlevel playing field.”  The hearing, largely a formality, will take place early November. Kallas, like most other commissioners-designate, is widely expected to be approved and start her new job as early as December.  In her statement, which was in answer to the European Parliament, Kallas also refers to China as one of a number of “malign” external actors, adding: “Actors such as Russia, Iran, North Korea and partly China, aim at weaponizing interdependencies and exploiting the openness of our societies against us. For this, we must be prepared.”  Other EU commissioners also call out China’s challenge: The Trade and Economic Security Commissioner-designate Maroš Šefčovič said he would talk to China — and sharpen EU tools — to address “significant level playing field concerns linked to the negative externalities of China’s state driven economic model and industrial policy, as well as the overcapacities that are distorting global markets and supply chains.” Even the Mediterranean Commissioner-designate Dubravka Šuica called out Beijing’s growing influence in the region, saying: “I am also fully conscious of the numerous challenges … Our rivals are making strides in the region. Countries such as China and Russia are imposing their own narratives and promoting their own interests, while the reputation of the EU is under pressure.”  EU takes a hawkish turn to climate ‘cooperation’ with China: China may have wanted the EU to play a more constructive role in keeping the climate dialogue open as one of the few remaining areas without hostilities. The EU’s incoming Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoestra, in his answers to Parliament, suggests that this won’t be the theme for the next five years.  “The [European] Commission has taken important steps to address dependencies on China, but more is needed,” he said. “ To ensure a level playing field for [EU industries], the Commission will also use trade defense instruments where justified, as it has done with the anti-subsidy measures on electric cars imported from China.”  HOT FROM THE CHINA WATCHERSPHERE  Photo Credit: Crossroads 社團法人台灣全球連結發展協會  Taiwan’s foreign residents seek citizenship  More than 5,000 foreign residents of Taiwan have signed an online petition urging the island’s government to drop the requirement that applicants for Taiwanese nationality renounce their existing citizenship.  Those signatures compiled over a 60-day period that concluded Sunday meet the regulatory requirement for submission of the petition to Taiwan’s government for an official response.  “Government agencies and policymakers have already been reaching out to us to learn more about our appeal,” said David Chang, secretary-general of the Taiwan-based nonprofit advocacy group Crossroads, which focuses on boosting the country’s internationalization. The petition now goes to the Ministry of Interior, but “what we are seeking will require the legislature to enact a bill amending the Nationality Act,” Chang said. Taiwan’s diplomatic outpost in Washington said that the ministry will respond to the petition by the end of November.  There are around one million foreign citizens — the majority laborers from Southeast Asia — in Taiwan with temporary or permanent residency status. U.S. citizens constitute around 15,000 of that total. Chang argues restrictions on Taiwanese citizenship hurt the island, saying the demographic challenges of a rapidly aging society deplete its workforce and the ranks of its military at a time of rising tensions across the Taiwan Strait.  But those foreigners — even those who have spent decades on the island and consider it home — can’t vote. And Taiwan has a thicket of rules restricting everything from certain jobs to subsidies for electrical scooter purchases to Taiwan citizens only. Taiwan also doesn’t have birthright citizenship, so children of foreign nationals born on the island have no route to becoming Taiwanese citizens.  “The harm that stems from being perennial outsiders is intangible, but it still hurts,” said Michael Turton, a U.S. citizen and columnist at the island’s Taipei Times newspaper, who has lived in Taiwan for more than two decades.  Support from Capitol Hill looks unlikely. “I understand how sensitive and how difficult those [citizenship] issues are. I don’t think it’s helpful for me to jump into a discussion” about them in Taiwan, said Rep. Mario Díaz-Balart (R-Fla.), a co-chair of the House Taiwan Caucus.  — MEET THE AXIS OF INDIGNATION: China insists its chumminess with dictators in North Korea, Russia and Iran doesn’t rate them being considered a hostile “axis.” That’s the message the Chinese Foreign Affairs Ministry sent out in an emailed statement Wednesday. It’s a response to the term “axis” seeping into a plethora of Washington think tanks’ assessments of Beijing’s ties with Tehran, Pyongyang and Moscow. They include the “axis of chaos,” axis of disorder, axis of revisionists and — with a nod to former President George W. Bush —a new “axis of evil.” Promoting “the ‘axis’ narrative will only exacerbate tensions in an already chaotic world, causing more conflicts and contradictions,” the statement said.  — MICROSOFT ISSUES CHINESE HACKER ALERT: Chinese hackers are joining counterparts from Iran and Russia in a potentially major influence operation ahead of the U.S. elections, Microsoft said in a report released Wednesday. The Chinese government-linked influence operation known as “Spamouflage” has “parroted antisemitic messages, amplified accusations of corruption and promoted opposition candidates,” the report said. Microsoft found that Spamouflage was spreading posts critical of Sen. Marsha Blackburn and Rep. Barry Moore (R-Ala.). POLITICO’s Maggie Miller has the full story here.  HEADLINES  Skift: Why are airlines quiet quitting China?  South China Morning Post: China’s 35 million ‘leftover men’ spark foreign brides idea to tackle gender imbalance  Wall Street Journal: Behind the mysterious downfall of China’s missing foreign minister  Bloomberg: In China, Harris is mostly seen as preferred to volatile Trump  ONE BOOK, THREE QUESTIONS  Taipei at Daybreak | Photo Credit: Rebecca Wright  The Book: Taipei at Daybreak  The Author: Brian Hioe is the founder of New Bloom Magazine which covers activism and youth politics in Taiwan  Responses have been edited for length and clarity.  Why did the world need an “American coming of age novel” set in Taipei, of all places?  The novel largely draws from my own background as someone caught between conflicting identities – Taiwanese and American — while not being simply one or the other. My own experiences are deeply bound up with the political upheavals that Taiwan went through around the time of the 2014 Sunflower Movement.  Taipei is more than just a backdrop for some story of personal discovery in the novel. The social and political context of Taipei in the early 2010s could be said to itself be a character in the story.  What role does Taiwan’s 2014 Sunflower Movement protests play in driving the novel’s plot?  The book centers around a number of social movements, including Occupy Wall Street in New York in 2011, the anti-nuclear protests that rocked Japan in 2012 in the wake of the Fukushima disaster, and the 2014 Sunflower Movement.  The most significant of these – for the protagonist and for myself – was the Sunflower Movement. That involved the youth-led occupation of the Taiwanese legislature in 2014 in protest of a trade deal that Taiwan’s then-government sought with China. It was a generational moment for Taiwanese young people and was a powerfully transformative moment in my own personal growth.  A subplot of the book is that the protagonist’s family members were complicit in Taiwan’s multi-decade “White Terror” period of authoritarian repression. Explain.  The many Asian American books and novels about Taiwan in recent years often come from a place of cultural pride — emphasizing resistance against past authoritarianism. But what does it mean to stand against authoritarianism but to have a family background tied to those who benefited from it?  This was something that many participants in the Sunflower Movement of “waishengren” [外省人- Chinese citizens who fled to Taiwan at the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949] descent grappled with in 2014, including myself. Opposition politician Ana Natsvlishvili from the Strong Georgia party said law enforcement authorities were idle, despite the fact that “organized criminal gangs … are trying to undermine the voting process with aggression and intimidation.”  Georgian President Salome Zourabichvili urged the Interior Ministry to remove criminals from polling places.  The ruling Georgian Dream party’s parliamentary leader, Mamuka Mdinaradze, speculated that an opposition TV channel might be “staging special operations” to create the impression of chaos.  A polling station in Marneuli, a town in southern Georgia, was closed down after a video circulated online showing a man, identified as a ruling party representative, stuffing a ballot box with dozens of ballots. description: Japan’s ruling coalition lost its majority in an election Sunday, leaving the world’s fourth-largest economy facing the prospect of minority governance or smaller parties acting as kingmakers in coalition talks.
text: Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba called a snap election less than a month ago upon assuming the leadership of the Liberal Democratic Party. | Tomohiro Ohsumi/Getty Images  New PM Shigeru Ishiba’s gamble on a snap election backfires, leaving him facing a fight to retain power.  Japan’s ruling coalition lost its majority in an election Sunday, leaving the world’s fourth-largest economy facing the prospect of minority governance or smaller parties acting as kingmakers in coalition talks.  Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba called a snap election less than a month ago upon assuming the leadership of the Liberal Democratic Party, which has ruled Japan for most of its post-war history.  But the move, which aimed to capitalize on a new-leader bounce and cement Ishiba’s credibility, backfired, with voters punishing the party for inflation and a funding scandal that led to the expulsion of some members.

text: Le briefing politique essentiel du matin.  Par SARAH PAILLOU  Avec ELISA BERTHOLOMEY  Envoyez vos infos | Abonnez-vous gratuitement | Voir dans le navigateur  PRESQUE NOËL. Nous sommes vendredi 25 octobre 2024, et Playbook a deux cadeaux pour illuminer votre week-end. Petit un, le nom d’une ministre de poids qui pourrait rejoindre la cause de Gabriel Attal, candidat encore officieux à la tête de Renaissance. Petit deux, révélé par POLITICO : le document qui liste les positions du gouvernement sur l’intégralité des amendements déposés sur la première partie du projet de loi de finances 2025, actuellement examinée à l’Assemblée nationale. Bon réveil à toutes et tous.  RENAISSANCE  DATI FAN D’ATTAL. Ne laissons pas le suspense durer plus longtemps : selon deux conseillers macronistes, Rachida Dati soutient le projet de Gabriel Attal de devenir le nouveau secrétaire général de Renaissance. “Si tu te présentes, j’adhère au parti !”, aurait même lancé la ministre de la Culture, aujourd’hui présidente du groupe Changer Paris au conseil de la capitale (et dont l’entourage n’a pas répondu à nos sollicitations nocturnes).  Les deux brouillés. Ce soutien supplémentaire — qu’il reste à officialiser — n’empêche pas qu’un obstacle de taille se dresse sur la route du trentenaire : les réticences (pour euphémiser) de l’Elysée, que vous conte Playbook depuis l’été. D’après son entourage, Emmanuel Macron craint de voir Renaissance devenir trop tôt une écurie au service d’ambitions présidentielles. Ce qui accélérerait, dans son esprit, les divisions du bloc central, voire le reniement de son bilan (rien à voir, donc, avec les relations ombrageuses qu’entretiennent les deux hommes).  L’entente cordiale. Notons sur ce point une inflexion dans la stratégie de Gabriel Attal. Mardi soir, Maxime Cordier, son homme de confiance, s’en est allé à l’Elysée rencontrer Jonathan Guémas, proche conseiller d’Emmanuel Macron, avait révélé Le Figaro. Les stratèges en sont convenus : il faut faire redescendre la tension entre les deux camps.  Hommage. Alors, les proches de Gabriel Attal distillent désormais des éléments de langage respectueux de l’héritage du père fondateur. L’une de ses soutiens nous le jurait en début de semaine, presque émouvante : “Sa démarche, depuis 2016, se fait derrière un homme qui est là, que nous n’oublions pas, grâce à qui nous sommes là et avec lequel nous voulons continuer à être là et à agir.” Un autre de ses interlocuteurs réguliers, moins lyrique, l’assurait hier : “S’il avait voulu vraiment la rupture, il aurait pu créer son parti comme Edouard Philippe.” Et de vanter son envie de prolongement du “dépassement” des clivages droite-gauche si cher au chef de l’Etat, et d’“unité” de la famille macroniste.  Félicitations du jury. Un fidèle du chef de l’Etat s’en satisfaisait en fin de matinée : “Gabriel a compris que le PR, faut pas non plus s’en faire un ennemi pour de vrai…”  NE FAIRE QU’UN. Les deux hommes se sont d’ailleurs revus en petit comité, pour la première fois depuis longtemps. Gabriel Attal était du déjeuner des huiles du camp présidentiel (raconté par Le Parisien), hier à l’Elysée. Emmanuel Macron a redit vouloir “tenir l’unité”, nous a glissé l’un des présents, qui “sentait bien qu’il y avait des tensions autour de la table”. A l’issue des agapes, le chef de l’Etat a retenu le président de groupe, ainsi qu’Elisabeth Borne, pour s’entretenir avec eux.  Aimez-vous. Un épisode de plus dans l’autre campagne (Playbook vous la chronique depuis plusieurs semaines, par exemple ici) : celle que mènent en coulisses le PR et son premier cercle pour tenter d’aboutir à une candidature unique. Un visiteur élyséen soupirait encore mardi devant nous : “L’affrontement de deux anciens Premiers ministres, au moment où c’est difficile pour les Français, en plein examen du budget, ça risque de faire du mal à tout le monde.”  Pourparlers. Entre les deux rivaux, ça continue à discuter, nous a-t-on confirmé hier dans chaque camp. Mais déjà, un soutien d’Attal dédramatisait le scénario dans lequel aucun accord n’était trouvé : “Il peut y avoir une élection et que ça se passe bien.”  CALENDRIER. Pour l’heure, à défaut d’être la candidate unique, Elisabeth Borne est l’unique candidate déclarée. Plusieurs bandes-annonces de l’officialisation de Gabriel Attal ont fleuri ces derniers jours dans la presse (ici ou là) à l’approche de la date limite de candidature (le 4 novembre). Sa déclaration, via un courrier aux adhérents, n’en finit pas d’être imminente. D’après l’un de ceux qui échangent avec son équipe, l’ancien Premier ministre compte lister les “valeurs” que le parti doit porter et faire des propositions “très concrètes” sur le fonctionnement de Renaissance, notamment en vue des élections municipales de 2026.  Pas si vite. Alors, c’est pour quand, c’est candidature ? Désormais, l’entourage d’Attal glisse qu’aucun calendrier n’est fixé. N’allez pas croire pour autant qu’il aurait renoncé à l’idée d’affronter Elisabeth Borne. Ou qu’il serait prêt à abandonner son poste actuel de président du groupe Ensemble pour la République (EPR) à l’Assemblée nationale, pour amadouer ses opposants vent debout contre un cumul avec la tête du parti. “Il restera président de groupe, il aime ça”, nous a encore martelé l’un de ses soutiens hier.  BUDGET 2025  SPOILER ALERT. Mon collègue Paul de Villepin a mis la main en exclusivité sur la version définitive du tableau des arbitrages gouvernementaux concernant les 3 500 modifications proposées par les députés sur la première partie du budget pour 2025. En clair, ce récap permet de savoir quelle sera la position du ministre du Budget et des Comptes publics, Laurent Saint-Martin, sur chaque amendement au projet de loi de finances, actuellement débattu à l’Assemblée nationale. A savoir : favorable, défavorable ou “de sagesse” (en gros, ni oui ni non).  Point jargon. En langage administratif, on appelle ce document azur un “bleu de RIM”, pour réunion interministérielle. En l’occurrence, celle de lundi à Matignon, en présence de toutes les administrations concernées par le budget. Ce tableau est le compte-rendu des décisions alors prises.  Leur préférence à eux. On découvre ainsi quelles idées des députés sont susceptibles d’être conservées dans la version finale du gouvernement, si Michel Barnier se décide à dégainer le 49.3, cet article de la Constitution qui permet l’adoption du PLF sans vote sur le texte. Mes collègues de Paris Influence vous proposent dans cet article (réservé à nos abonnés pro) un aperçu des préférences de l’exécutif, par exemple sur le soutien à l’innovation, des retouches du crédit d’impôt recherche ou encore une TVA réduite sur les chaudières à gaz.  Ce n’est pas tout : le bleu de RIM nous indique aussi quels groupes parlementaires ont les égards de l’exécutif. And the winner is… la majorité gouvernementale (étonnamment), et surtout Ensemble pour la République (ex-Renaissance). Sur les 114 amendements validés lundi à Matignon (incluant aussi ceux du rapporteur général du budget, Charles de Courson, qui se veulent parfois la synthèse des idées des députés), 27 émanent d’EPR, 16 de Droite républicaine (ex-Les Républicains), 11 du MoDem et neuf d’Horizons. Le groupe Liot pourra se targuer d’avoir convaincu sur six de ses propositions (sans compter celles de Courson), les socialistes deux, tout comme le RN ainsi que l’UDR d’Eric Ciotti.  DÉLESTAGE. Hier soir, le ministère des Relations avec le Parlement a acté que les députés siégeraient samedi pour tenter de venir à bout de leurs travaux, avant le vote solennel de mardi. Sur les plus de 2 400 amendements encore à examiner, “le gouvernement estime que 1 000 sont gérables”, nous a glissé à un pilier du Palais-Bourbon. “A charge pour chacun des groupes de faire le job”, poursuivait-il.  Comprendre : l’exécutif espère que les députés retireront une partie de leurs propositions pour accélérer les débats, comme l’ont déjà fait hier La France insoumise et EPR. Au sein du groupe de Gabriel Attal, on diffusait dans la soirée, comme preuve de bonne volonté, un tableau montrant qu’EPR n’avait plus que 3,7 amendements par député ; contre 13,5 pour les troupes de Laurent Wauquiez.  À SUIVRE AUSSI AUJOURD’HUI  DANS LE MÊME BATEAU. Michel Barnier et Agnès Pannier-Runacher se rendent dans le Rhône aujourd’hui, une semaine après que le département a été touché par de fortes intempéries. C’est la première fois que le chef du gouvernement et sa ministre de la Transition écologique se déplacent conjointement après les critiques formulées par la seconde sur son budget, qu’elle avait jugé “pas à la hauteur de la situation”. “Ils vont avoir le temps de mettre les choses au clair”, s’amusait, hier matin, un bon connaisseur des sujets écolo.  Pnacc trop tôt. Cette première sortie sur le thème de l’environnement pour Michel Barnier servira surtout de prétexte à la présentation du troisième plan national d’adaptation au changement climatique (Pnacc). Le dévoilement de ces 51 mesures, déjà ficelées avant la dissolution, avait été moult fois retardé, rappelle dans Energie et Climat (pour nos abonnés Pro) ma collègue Aude Le Gentil. Qui vous raconte tout des enjeux… financiers, encore une fois, de ce dossier.  EN CHAMBRE  MÉNAGE BRETON. Trop c’est trop, juge Xavier Breton. Le député Droite républicaine (ex-Les Républicains), à la tête de la délégation du bureau de l’Assemblée nationale chargée des groupes d’études, entend diminuer drastiquement le nombre de ces instances supposées aider les députés à “approfondir des questions spécifiques”, sans vrai but législatif. Le vice-président du Palais-Bourbon voudrait donc diminuer leur nombre de 80 à 58, a-t-il fait savoir aux chefs de groupe, dans un courrier daté du 16 octobre, habilement récupéré et dévoilé hier dans Paris Influence à nos abonnés Pro par ma collègue Anne-Charlotte Dusseaulx.  Ce serait bien de bosser. Déjà, fin septembre, Yaël Braun-Pivet faisait part, dans une autre missive aux mêmes destinataires, d’un “constat” partagé avec elle par Breton : “une quinzaine de groupes d’études [n’a] eu, après leur réunion constitutive, qu’une activité très réduite voire nulle” sous la précédente législature. Les sujets de travaux choisis ne doivent “pas traduire l’expression d’un intérêt trop étroit”, écrivait encore la présidente de l’Assemblée nationale. Avant la dissolution, on en trouvait sur des thématiques aussi variées que la Camargue, l’amiante, les Ouïghours ou le thermalisme.  Faites vos vœux. Les députés ont donc été priés de faire remonter les sujets prioritaires à leurs yeux. Et certains voudraient… ouvrir de nouveaux champs. Ainsi les socialistes défendent-ils l’idée d’un groupe d’études sur la santé des femmes, qu’ils aimeraient voir présidé par l’ancien ministre Aurélien Rousseau. Les Insoumis, eux, aimeraient créer les instances suivantes : “racisme et discriminations”, “journalisme, presse et droit à l’information”, “enjeux des technologies quantiques” et “grands projets impactants”. Breton espère officialiser la nouvelle liste “d’ici la fin de cette année”, écrit-il dans son courrier. description: By contrast, Starmer scrapped the Rwanda plan and leans into green projects beloved of the king. While Charles has to be strictly neutral on party politics, he has a sense of “compassion, social cohesion,” said Dimbleby.
text: Charles, too, has mellowed his well-known views on issues such as climate change and housing, at least in public, as part of the strict convention of neutrality that comes with being king.  His style in the past was far from laid back. One former minister recalled Charles, as prince of Wales, inviting them for tea at St James’s Palace, where they found themselves discussing policy for more than an hour. A second ex-minister recalled the future king questioning ministers on the detail of green finance — though never in a way that would lobby for a policy, they insisted. While he would occasionally “raise eyebrows” in private, they said, “what he will do is come up with ideas or offers. He will say, ‘This group of people deserve a pat on the back — would it be helpful to you, minister, if I did an event with them or I send you something on that?’”  ‘He pulled me to one side’  George Brandis, Australia’s former high commissioner to the U.K., recalls how the then-prince of Wales was “very eager to see” Australia commit to a target of net zero carbon emissions by 2050. When Canberra did — days before the COP26 climate summit in 2021 — “Charles was delighted about that. He had made it pretty clear on a number of occasions that he was very much hoping that Australia would do that. In fact, as I read it, [he] was a bit impatient that we hadn’t done so until relatively late in the piece.”  Brandis added: “He is obviously very conscious of the constitutional limitations of his role as king, and I’m sure that his public or private advocacy of causes will be much less in evidence now that he is on the throne. But nevertheless … I found him very determined to make his views known and to be an advocate for the causes he deeply cares about, particularly environmental ones.”  That does not make the king humorless; like Starmer, he is said to be warm and cracks jokes in private. Charles also shows “strong emotions,” more than his late mother, said Dimbleby: “He can get very frustrated, and those around him sometimes see that. They also see his total commitment to issues that matter and his ability to speak in a very informed way about them, and in private he feels perfectly free to do that.”  In September 2023, a year almost to the day after his own mother’s death, the king wrote a deeply personal letter to then-Defence Secretary Grant Shapps, who had recently lost his father. Shapps told POLITICO: “He left it on my bed at Dumfries House [a royal residence in Scotland]. It was a beautifully written, hand-annotated letter from the king. Later, when I went downstairs for dinner, he pulled me to one side and said, ‘I know that there are no words that can match losing a parent, but I do hope you found my letter.’ … He is an unbelievably thoughtful man, and it was a heartfelt thing for him to do.”

text: Lebanon, a former French protectorate, has long been marred by war, corruption, internal political strife and economic malaise. The situation has been particularly dire since the 2020 explosion at an ammunition factory in Beirut, the capital, which killed more than 200 people and caused an estimated $15 billion in property damage.  Macron said France’s donation went toward an initial target of €500 million set for the conference. He added that the massive injection of cash was needed to take care of those who have fled the fighting, many from southern Lebanon, and to prevent infighting between locals and the displaced population.  Macron used his speech to blame both Israel and Hezbollah’s regional backer Iran for the plight of the Lebanese. He called on Hezbollah to “cease its provocations,” whether attacks against Netanyahu’s home or “indiscriminate attacks” on Israel.  He also called on Israel to accept a cease-fire with Hezbollah, adding that “Israel knows its military successes do not lead to victory” in Lebanon, referencing Israel’s multiple invasions of its neighbor. Macron has also called for a cease-fire between Israel and Hamas in Gaza.  While Macron took aim at the divided leaders of Israel, Iran and Lebanon in his speech, his position on the Middle East has been hard to follow since the Oct. 7 attack on Israel led by Hamas.  The French president and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have also traded barbs recently over Israel’s refusal to move toward a cease-fire.

Austin said the U.S. is also still attempting to determine what North Korea will get in return for helping Russia with manpower.  NATO spokesperson Farah Dakhlallah said in an emailed statement Wednesday afternoon that: “Allies have confirmed evidence of a DPRK troop deployment to Russia. If these troops are destined to fight in Ukraine, it would mark a significant escalation in North Korea’s support for Russia’s illegal war and yet another sign of Russia’s significant losses on the front lines.  "We are actively consulting within the Alliance on this matter, and the North Atlantic Council will receive a briefing from the Republic of Korea and further discuss this matter soon,” the spokesperson added.  Kyiv has already published a video address to DPRK troops, calling on soldiers to surrender as soon as they are deployed to fight in Ukraine.  “You should not die senselessly on someone else's land. There is no need to repeat the fate of hundreds of thousands of Russian soldiers who will never return home! Surrender in captivity! Ukraine will shelter, feed and warm you,” staff from Ukraine's prisoner of war (POW) hotline said in a video statement in Korean on Wednesday.

text: A government official, granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive matter, confirmed that policy pertaining to China — including the FIRS scheme — had been put on pause until the government completes its ongoing “China Audit,” expected to wrap early next year.  A tit-for-tat row erupted last week after Labour’s Security Minister Dan Jarvis blamed the delay on the previous Conservative government.  He claimed they had “completely failed to put in the appropriate measures” to implement the scheme, and that the IT solution for the register was “not yet ready.”  Tom Tugendhat said that, even accounting for the U.K.’s general election, there was no reason for the scheme not to be introduced before the end of this year. | Photo by Carl Court/Getty Images  His comments came after his Conservative predecessor Tom Tugendhat wrote to Prime Minister Keir Starmer to question the delay, saying he had been ready to launch the scheme in autumn 2024. Tugendhat said that, even accounting for the U.K.’s general election, there was no reason for the scheme not to be introduced before the end of this year.  Conservative MP Alicia Kearns, who formerly chaired the House of Commons foreign affairs committee tasked with scrutinizing the government, told POLITICO the “necessary preparation work” was completed “well ahead” of the election, and branded Labour’s claims “totally unfounded.”  She argued Labour’s “softening stance” on China was to blame. Foreign Secretary David Lammy made a rare, low-key visit to Beijing last week as part of a wider diplomatic push to rethink economic and political links with the country.

text: While he says that “work should continue on food labeling,” it’s unclear whether he’s referring to national or European efforts, and he wants “particular attention on minimizing any related burdens (for industry) ... finding balanced, pragmatic solutions which facilitate the functioning of the internal market.”  And on a question whether he would commit to delivering promised booze health labels, Várhelyi dodged it entirely.  To many health NGOs, as well as lawmakers, dropping mandatory labels would be a blow. Progress on EU-wide preventative measures — including food and booze labels — is critical to tackle these growing disease rates, and “should be a key focus for the next mandate,” the Socialists and Democrats argued earlier this month.  Under current EU rules, countries do not have to provide front-of-pack nutritional information. | Nicolas Guyonnet/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images  "The functioning of the internal market should not be used as an excuse not to take action on food and alcohol labelling," Caroline Costongs, director of EuroHealthNet, a partnership for improving health and social equity, said.  She called for "a bold commitment to an EU-wide standardization of food labelling such as Nutri-Score, which is a proven effective and an essential step forward to tackle obesity and NCDs," and added that consumers also "have a right to know what is in an alcoholic drink."  What happened to food and booze labels?  Under current EU rules, countries do not have to provide front-of-pack nutritional information. But a proposal for a mandatory EU-wide nutrition label was first introduced in 2020 by the European Commission as part of its Farm to Fork Strategy.

text: Speaking to POLITICO, Giorgi Oniani, the deputy director of Transparency International in Georgia, said the anti-corruption watchdog had analyzed more than 360 photos and video recordings of irregularities during polling on Saturday, as well as detailed statistical data from more than 100 of the 1,131 polling stations across the country.  “On paper, Georgian Dream’s majority of 400,000 votes looks significant. But when you break it down by polling precincts, together with other schemes, it could have been down to flipping fewer than 100 opposition votes in each district,” he said.  “In practice, we’ve seen evidence Georgian Dream has used the state security apparatus to carry out a massive program of voter surveillance to target opposition-minded Georgians for vote buying and intimidation schemes,” Oniani said.  An Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe-led international monitoring mission said the vote was “marred by an uneven playing field, pressure and tension, but voters were offered a wide choice” of candidates.  “Election results do not represent the will of the Georgian people,” said Giorgi Gakharia, former chairman of the opposition For Georgia bloc. | Lex Van Lieshout/Getty Images  Fears of media crackdown  Transparency International is one of the civil society groups that will be branded a “foreign agent” under a new Russian-style law targeting Western-funded NGOs, which was passed by Georgian Dream MPs over the summer despite widespread protests. It has said it will refuse to comply, and could be shuttered in the coming months if authorities push ahead with enforcement.  Other organizations have raised fears of a crackdown on the media. In a statement, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) warned that “Georgia’s drift away from democracy is now eroding one of its core pillars: press freedom,” adding that threats, harassment and legal challenges were squeezing independent media.

text: Good Monday morning. This is Sam Blewett.  DRIVING THE DAY  FIRE BURN AND CAULDRON BUBBLE: Keir Starmer will use a major speech this morning to warn Britain must embrace the “harsh light of fiscal reality” ahead of Chancellor Rachel Reeves’ first budget this week. The prime minister will attempt to get ahead of looming criticism of the £40 billion of tax hikes and spending cuts set to be unveiled on the eve of Halloween — promising there will be “better days” ahead as he adds a dash of positivity into a largely gloomy mix. But there’s an unwelcome distraction threatening to derail the prime minister’s messaging today, after Labour suspended an MP on Sunday evening over a witching hour altercation.  Put down the broomstick: Barely 24 hours after returning from his Samoan sojourn and Starmer is off on his travels again, this time to the West Midlands to roll the pitch ahead of Wednesday’s budget. Kicking off at 11.15 a.m., the PM will be promising a package of investment in the NHS, schools and infrastructure and pledging no return to austerity. He’ll also vow to “protect working people’s payslips” — but don’t necessarily expect a clear explanation of whom that affects. Playbook hears there will be a new policy in the speech too, though the details are still under wraps.  Step away from the abyss: Expect plenty of blaming the Tories for that £22 billion “black hole” in the budget — though Starmer will insist he won’t be using the state of the economy as an “excuse.” He’ll say: “Politics is always a choice. It’s time to choose a clear path, and embrace the harsh light of fiscal reality so we can come together behind a credible, long-term plan.” Downing Street’s trail of the speech makes plenty of front pages this morning.  **A message from Google: Research with Public First revealed that AI is set to enhance 74% of roles across the education sector and could help the sector to unlock a productivity boost worth £31bn. That’s why our AI Works programme is partnering with schools, to deliver AI training for teachers, allowing them to spend more time on what matters. Learn more: goo.gle/ai-works-edu-uk**  Quizzing Keir: Starmer’s speech will be followed by a press Q&A. Expect plenty of questions on all the new titbits about the budget which emerged in the weekend’s papers.  The tricks: A mooted ditching of the £2 cap on bus fares that’ll likely go down just as badly with regional Labour mayors as it will with passengers. That, on top of the National Insurance hike for employers and the freezing of income tax bands — measures which also somehow didn’t make it into the Labour manifesto — is unlikely to quell the growing cynicism among voters, which the i paper puts on its front page.  The treats: The Mail’s Jason Groves reports that Reeves will announce a “significant” rise in the minimum wage, to be rebranded the “new living wage.” The move would be welcomed by hundreds of thousands of low earners — though businesses may have a fair few concerns, particularly considering it would come on top of the planned hike in employers’ NICs. The Sun’s Ryan Sabey also hears Reeves will pledge £500 million extra for fixing potholes.  Monetary myxomatosis: One senior Labour official was well and truly trying to downplay any big shocks coming on Wednesday — no doubt wary of further fueling jitters in the bond markets over Reeves’ plans for greater borrowing to fund capital spending. “The era of budget rabbits is over,” the official told Playbook. “We’re ending austerity and we’re ending rabbits.” Eek.  Sending out the big guns: Pat McFadden is the warm-up act for Starmer’s speech. The Cabinet Office bigwig is handling the morning broadcast round right now, including the Today program’s 8.10 a.m. slot.  HELP! WE’VE OPENED 5 NEW FREEPORTS BY MISTAKE: One thing ministers won’t be all too keen to discuss are freeports. The government was forced into an embarrassing climbdown at the weekend after committing to opening five more of the low-tax zones — in error. The FT’s Peter Foster and Jim Pickard got the scoop that there won’t in fact be any new freeports at all coming in the budget. My colleague Esther Webber hears officials hurriedly tried to secure a correction when the announcement was made last Friday — however, the whole thing was snarled up by the fact that Starmer and his aides (who’d trailed the news) were 13 hours ahead in Samoa.  One for the ages: It’s quite the “comms cock up,” as one government official lamented to Playbook. (Similar comments were made to the FT and the BBC, suggesting there’s at least one very unhappy bunny in Whitehall.) Officials say Reeves will merely be giving the go-ahead to new customs sites at five of the existing freeports — and are baffled as to how No. 10 accidentally managed to upgrade that announcement to the creation of five entirely new freeports.  Time for (another) reset: Claire Reynolds, the director of Labour Women’s Network who served as an aide to both Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, has been appointed by Starmer as his new political director in Downing Street. The Guardian’s Kiran Stacey and Pippa Crerar, who got the scoop last night, point out she’s married to Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds — installing the pair high up in the ranks of Westminster’s (many) power couples. My ace colleague Annabelle Dickson (who compiles POLITICO’s legendary annual list) will be sharpening her quill.  No one said this was going to be easy: Research outfit More in Common will give a briefing today on the budget bind Labour finds itself in, with research suggesting 53 percent of people believe the priority should be keeping taxes low, compared to 32 percent who want investment in public services prioritized. Then there’s the polling suggesting a whopping 70 percent of the public reckon things are getting worse, with only 7 percent believing they’re improving. Tune in from 10.30 a.m. here.  Making the case: Economic evangelists in the Labour Growth Group — a new pro-Starmer caucus of backbench MPs — are meeting with businesses in Westminster this evening to support what they reckon can be a “revolution in investment” in the U.K. But there’s more discontent in other quarters.  VATs entertainment: Firstly, France and Germany are furious at Labour’s plans to hit private school fees with VAT, due to the impact on international schools here in the U.K. Hélène Duchêne and Miguel Berger, the nations’ ambassadors to the U.K., argued to the FT and the Times that international schools should be treated differently and that slapping VAT on their fees will damage diplomatic relations with Britain. Duchêne tells the papers the plan is “not in line with the reset to our relationship which the British government has instigated.”  One person who’s really not happy … is Jeremy Hunt. The former chancellor has criticized the Office for Budget Responsibility for reportedly planning to publish an assessment of the £22 billion “black hole” he’s accused of leaving behind. Hunt has written to OBR Chair Richard Hughes saying the review (and a failure to consult with him) is not “consistent with political impartiality” and “would cross a line.” The Telegraph splashes on his angry missive.  ANGER FROM THE LEFT TOO: Labour backbenchers Diane Abbott, Bell Ribeiro-Addy and Clive Lewis have accused Starmer of possessing a “colonial mindset” over his reluctance to discuss reparations for slavery at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, Donna Ferguson reports in the Guardian. Starmer is not planning a statement to the Commons on the standoff in Samoa, but Foreign Secretary David Lammy is expected in the House this afternoon to discuss the worsening picture in the Middle East.  DERAILING THE MESSAGE: Labour was forced into firefighting mode last night after the Mail Online published footage apparently showing MP for Runcorn and Helsby Mike Amesbury punching a man to the ground before continuing to hit him as he lies in the street. The party announced that Amesbury has had his membership suspended pending investigation, meaning he loses the Labour whip in the Commons too.  ICYMI: Footage first emerged over the weekend of Amesbury shouting at a man lying on the street in Frodsham, in his Cheshire constituency, at around 2.15 a.m on Saturday morning. “You won’t threaten the MP ever again, will you,” Amesbury said. The MP released a statement saying he’d spoken to the police after the incident “following an evening out with friends.” Labour initially stood back, insisting it was a matter for the police.  Content warning: The Mail published its genuinely shocking CCTV footage showing actual punches being thrown. Playbook hears Amesbury (who has been the victim of stalking in the past) had given some sort of explanation to Labour officials — but they decided to take action only after the new footage emerged. It’s unclear what led up to the incident.  By-election calls: Tory leadership candidate Robert Jenrick slid two feet in to attack Labour over the incident, while Reform UK called for Amesbury to “do the honorable thing and resign” so a by-election can be held. Nigel Farage’s outfit came in second in the constituency at the general election 14,696 votes behind Labour — a large majority, but hardly a test Starmer would embrace considering the circumstances.  Unwanted coverage: The incident made the BBC News at Ten bulletin last night behind only war in the Middle East, while the story splashes the Daily Mail today and makes the front pages of the Guardian, the Times and the Telegraph. Safe to say a street-brawling MP is one of the last things Labour would want to be talking about as it prepares to unveil its first budget in 14 years.  PLANET TORY  THE END IS NIGH: It’s the final week of a Tory leadership race which feels like it’s been dragging on forever — and Kemi Badenoch and Robert Jenrick are still duking it out to win the coveted prize of the “worst job in politics,” a.k.a the leader of the opposition.  Live from the culture war: Badenoch (who’s picked up the endorsement of former Attorney General Geoffrey Cox for taking on the “theologians of woke”) will take questions from the Mumsnet forum from 10 a.m. (details here). She’ll swing by BBC Radio 2 for an interview and then head to the Commons in her guise as shadow housing secretary to face Angela Rayner in the Commons for departmental questions at 2.30 p.m.  Hardly a day of rest: Badenoch and Jenrick spent Sunday exchanging a series of barbs. It started with Badenoch making an ever-so-thinly-veiled attack by pointing out in an interview with the Sunday Telegraph that she’d “never been sacked” amid a “whiff of impropriety.” Whoever could she have been referring to … surely not her opponent, who left Boris Johnson’s government in 2021 after a planning controversy centering on Conservative donor Richard Desmond?  Ref! Ref! Jenrick struck back on GB News, calling the remarks “garbage” and arguing that Badenoch’s behavior could be “the death of the Conservative Party.” The yellow card system that party chiefs hoped would maintain some decorum in the contest has not been used so far — but these are the most open attacks by the candidates to date.  It’s all food for thought: Tory party members have until 5 p.m. Thursday to cast their votes. Rishi Sunak, who will respond to the budget for the Conservatives in one of his last major acts in the Commons, will be relieved of his duties when the winner is announced on Saturday. It seems even Tory activists are struggling to engage, with the Sun’s Harry Cole hearing that as of Friday less than half of Tory members had voted, with insiders suspecting turnout will be way down on 2022 (those giddy days when Conservative activists got to select the actual prime minister).  For the winner, 15 minutes of fame: The party’s timetable for the election means that any attention the newly crowned leader does garner will be quickly curtailed by a leadership election the world actually cares about — with voters going to the polls in America three days later. Safe to say Kamala Harris vs. Donald Trump continues to put the old Bobby J-Kemi B contest into perspective.  LAST NIGHT IN NEW YORK  WHILE YOU WERE SLEEPING: Donald Trump’s rally at Madison Square Garden was drawing furious condemnation after the event opened with a racist diatribe. Just nine days out from the Nov. 5 election, the glitzy campaign stop had been billed as a triumphant homecoming to New York for the former president, but it quickly descended into a political fiasco that even prominent Republicans criticized.  From the off: The event in the heart of Manhattan opened with comedian Tony Hinchcliffe, the host of the “Kill Tony” podcast, making a series of slurs about Latinos, African Americans and other quarters of society that the Republican campaign is targeting to turn out for Trump. “There’s literally a floating island of garbage in the middle of the ocean right now. I think it’s called Puerto Rico,” he told the audience. My colleagues in D.C. have more on his remarks and the backlash here.  Not us, guv: A Trump adviser said the comments weren’t vetted by the campaign, but the Republican went on to reprise some of his harshest remarks about immigration as his supporters chanted “send them back.” Trump reiterated his calls to weed out “the enemy from within” and called for the death penalty for “any migrant who kills an American citizen.” He vowed to “end inflation” and “stop the invasion of criminals coming into our country.”  The cast: The rally featured a succession of Trump offspring and even an appearance by the lesser-spotted Melania Trump, along with the nowadays regular Elon Musk. Some Democrats, including vice-presidential pick Tim Walz, compared the event to an infamous 1939 Nazi rally at Madison Square Garden — but wrestler Hulk Hogan (after ripping off a Trump tank top and removing his red and yellow boa) growled to the crowd: “You know something Trumpmaniacs, I don’t see no stinking Nazis in here.”  MEANWHILE, IN PHILADELPHIA: Kamala Harris spent the day in Pennsylvania’s largest city. The Democrat’s campaign fears that if she fails to drive turnout among Black and Latino voters there, then she’ll lose both the state and her clearest path to the White House. Recent polling suggests Trump has been cutting into Harris’ margins among Black and Latino men.  Preach, Kamala: From the pulpit of a largely Black church to a barbershop chair and a Puerto Rican restaurant, Harris warned voters that Trump is “full of grievance” and would harm them and their families if he regained the presidency, as my POLITICO colleague Meredith Lee Hill writes in her coverage here.  (On the) Streets of Philadelphia: Former President Barack Obama and Bruce Springsteen will be on stage at a Harris rally in North Philadelphia from 8 p.m. tonight. At a recent Georgia rally, Springsteen took to the stage to say Trump is running to be an “American tyrant.”  The verdict: My U.S. colleague Adam Wren writes that if Trump does end up losing the election, then the “racist carnival” at Madison Square Garden could well be remembered as the day that did it. As Adam points out, nearly half a million people of Puerto Rican descent live in the battleground state of Pennsylvania. Read his analysis here.  But but but: Trump and his allies have long said these sorts of things and the polls have this race pretty much neck-and-neck.  **Don't miss your chance to attend the Financial Services UK Summit, where industry leaders, policymakers, and innovators come together to discuss the future of financial services. Brussels announced on Friday that it would take the U.K. to court over London’s prohibition on fishing the species, which was brought in by the last Tory government to protect endangered seabirds including puffins. It’s among the wave of suggestions submitted to the Commons modernization committee, along with earlier sitting hours and digital voting. Read Esther’s piece here. description: Pricing nature is the holy grail of biodiversity policy. If governments can get the capitalist system to put a dollar value on the riches of nature, proponents argue it could be key to halting and reversing devastating biodiversity loss.As with carbon pricing, it would force the market to solve the problem, saving governments a lot of money and effort.
text: Bachmann said the law aims to address a lot of the criticisms of trading nature. For example, while the rules allow developers to buy units from other sites, they include a financial incentive to buy credits generated near the construction site. The further away the project, the more units you need. This attempts to make sure ecosystem destruction in one location is not offset by restoration of an entirely different ecosystem in another part of the world.  It also has different grades of units, from those representing simple grasslands, to much more complex ecosystems such as forests or wetlands — in an effort to address concerns that biodiversity credits artificially homogenize something as diverse and place-specific as nature.  Because of all this, Bachmann believes BNG is a global paragon for creating a compliance market in nature credits.  Who will police it?  But not everyone is convinced. "There’s been a lot of hype about biodiversity net gain," said Paul de Zylva, a senior nature campaigner with Friends of the Earth. "It’s certainly a world first. Whether it’s world leading is yet to be proven."  De Zylva worries that the U.K. government simply has not put aside the necessary resources and expertise to monitor and enforce the rules. And as yet, there is no centralized watchdog to make sure the regime functions properly.  But even if compliance questions were answered — a big "if" according to de Zylva — he still has philosophical objections to the notion of pricing nature.

text: Good afternoon. This is Andrew McDonald in Westminster, with Dan Bloom filing from Samoa.  THURSDAY’S CHEAT SHEET  — Rachel Reeves confirmed she plans to change her fiscal rules in next week’s budget.  — All the latest from Samoa as Keir Starmer prepares to hobnob with Commonwealth leaders.  — Ed Balls (and a whole plethora of Tories) hit out at Labour’s handling of its row with Donald Trump.  — Starmer has never used a disposable vape, apparently.  **A message from Lloyds Banking Group: At Lloyds Banking Group we believe everyone deserves a safe and warm place to call home. That’s why we’ve joined with the National Wealth Fund to deliver £500 million in funding to retrofit social homes across the UK. Find out more here.**  TOP OF THE NEWSLIST  LET’S GET FISCAL: The worst kept secret in Westminster is out — Rachel Reeves is changing her fiscal rules next week.  Look what you made me do: Wearing what looked like a Taylor Swift bracelet in Washington D.C. this morning, the chancellor confirmed to reporters including POLITICO’s Emilio Casalicchio — who he? — that she will indeed tweak the U.K.’s fiscal rules on investment in the budget.  Not spilling: Reeves is keeping the specifics a secret until Oct. 30 — in a bid to avoid raising the hackles of the Commons speaker, it seems. “I can confirm today that we will be changing the way that we measure debt in the budget statement next week, but I’ll set out the details of that to parliament,” Reeves said.  Some non-specific deets: In a sit-down with BBC News — more lines from her round of interviews with economic editors will be popping up as you read this email — Reeves said she would change “the measure of debt” aimed at helping to increase investment levels in the U.K. Theoretically, this frees up £50 billion in headroom for the chancellor to play with.  New chancellor, new rules: Jeremy Hunt’s rules, which he brought in after the whole Liz Truss crashing the economy thing, meant day-to-day spending had to be met by revenues, and that debt as a share of the economy needed to be falling in the fifth year of forecasts produced by the Office for Budget Responsibility. The rules were criticized by some think tanks for being too restrictive, leading to “short term-ism” in policymaking.  In the pinko: Reeves announcement came alongside an op-ed in the FT aimed at cooling any market anguish and calming the nerves of bond traders. She pointed to “guardrails” that would ensure prudent spending, including new oversight bodies.  But unfortunately: The markets were already moving following the Guardian’s overnight scoop on the new rules. Yields on British government bonds climbed this morning by about six points — which, for the non-economists reading, is a bad thing, BTW. Reeves insisted to reporters her plans should not spook the markets.  After speaking to reporters … Reeves skipped off to the IMF summit in central D.C. to hobnob with her new foreign fiscal friends. Reeves attended the G20 finance ministers and central banking meeting, another G20 meeting about climate, and is now having a few bilats with fellow cash controllers. There will be pics on the HMT Flickr account. Officials are keeping tight-lipped on whether she could meet folks from the U.S. presidential campaigns while she’s in D.C. but stress her focus is on the IMF.  WHILE SEVERAL TIME ZONES AWAY: It’s almost dawn and a jet-lagged Keir Starmer has finally slept off his 27-hour flight … ish (Dan Bloom writes). After a brief pit stop to see hacks at a riverside burger joint, the PM was finally free to hit the sack. Not for long though — he’ll be awake any moment to prep for broadcast interviews with the BBC, ITV and Sky as CHOGM continues in Samoa. Brace for lines on the budget, Donald Trump, reparations and more to appear at 10 p.m. U.K. time.  See me: Starmer will meet four leaders of fellow Commonwealth countries — due to be Australia, Samoa, Ghana and Guyana — and attend two “executive sessions,” at which he’ll talk about growth and the like. However, some of the leaders will try to pin him down in those same sessions on the small matter of reparations for the slave trade. Bahamas PM Philip Davis told Dan he wants a “frank talk” with Starmer, who he worked alongside on human rights issues more than 20 years ago. Interview here.  Rumbling on: Dan hears Downing Street’s blunt “not on the agenda” response to calls for reparations has caused ire among Caribbean countries — especially given CHOGM is a pretty free-flowing affair, including a six-hour unstructured leaders’ retreat with no aides.  But that said: Dan also hears the final text of the communique — a draft of which referred directly to reparations — is not nailed down, and there is still the possibility that the R-word could be hived off into a separate declaration.  ROYAL JUMBLE: Meanwhile it’s King Charles day at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, which will happen while you’re asleep — leaders who’ve bothered to come arrive from 9.30 p.m. and the main event is from 11.15 p.m. U.K. time, with a speech by the monarch (get out your climate change bingo card). Charles then hosts lunch for new heads of government *and* dinner for wider heads of government. Starmer will be at both.  The dangers of “business casual”: Even Starmer’s healthily-stocked wardrobe doesn’t stretch to Samoa’s proliferation of flowery gear. The opening banquet was billed to delegations as a relaxed island-style affair, so Starmer duly removed his tie. He sat next to Aussie PM Anthony Albanese, who was wearing … a tropical shirt and shorts (h/t pool reporter David Lynch from PA).  DRIVETIME DEBRIEF  BACK IN BLIGHTY: Starmer’s opponents are still trying to make hay out of Donald Trump’s moans about Labour staff campaigning for the Democrats.  Wading in today: Tory leadership contender Robert Jenrick — on yet another morning media round — told Sky News the row “risks the U.K.’s relationship” with the (possible) future president, while Tory MP Andrew Snowden told POLTICO’s Noah Keate that the campaigning has “back-fired and will probably help Trump now.”  Balls-up: This one might sting a bit more. Former Labour Shadow Chancellor Ed Balls told his podcast with his bezzie mate George Osborne that Labour has been “naive and gauche” … and that an “alarm bell” should have rung when an official in the party of government started “organizing a sort of posse of campaigners as a foreign party.”  But don’t worry Keir: Nigel Farage reckons his big pal Trump will eventually forgive Keir Starmer despite Labour officials campaigning for Kamala Harris. So that’s nice. Farage was speaking to Times Radio.  Still firefighting: On her morning round earlier, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy distanced herself from Kamala Harris’ description of Trump as a fascist — as Labour tries to hose down the rammy with her opponent. Noah has a write-up of that one.  What she wanted to talk about: Nandy played down frictions with the Premier League as she talked up the government’s new football governance measures. Unfortunately for her, the Premier League is still pretty mad — saying last night the bill “could have a negative impact on the league’s continued competitiveness.” Which sounds a lot like … friction.  NO VAPE NATION: No. 10 insisted its upcoming ban on disposable vapes is not another example of nanny-state policy making — after announcing plans to ban the sale of disposable vapes in England and Wales from June next year. “I wouldn’t characterize it that way,” the PM’s deputy official spokesperson said. “This is the right action to protect children’s health while balancing the necessary preparations of such a significant step.”  As for whether Starmer has ever used an elf bar … his spokesperson said they “weren’t aware” of any disposable puffing from the PM.  SAY IT AIN’T SO: Sales of Boris Johnson’s memoir have slumped by 62 percent in its second week. To be fair, it does still hold the No. 1 spot in the U.K. top 50 charts. The Guardian’s Aletha Adu has a write-up.  CHEAPER BAILOUTS: Councils struggling with their dosh will no longer be required to pay a premium on financial bailouts, DPM Angela Rayner announced as she addressed the Local Government Association. Here’s PA’s write-up.  On that note: Both the New Statesman and the Spectator have pieces out on the rise of Rayner’s influence in government — Katy Balls describes it as her “resurgence”, while George Eaton calls it a “renaissance.” Choose your own adventure!  UNHAPPY READING FOR THE PM: YouGov finds Starmer has a worse PM job rating than all of his predecessors by this point in their tenure … except for Liz Truss, who never made it this far of course. But the data is maybe most interesting in the way it shows the decline of the “honeymoon period” over the last decade and a half, with more recent PMs becoming unpopular far quicker than their predecessors.  Meanwhile in the Lords: Former PM Theresa May made her maiden speech in the other place — making what one witness in the chamber described as a “classy, very relaxed” speech without notes on modern slavery and the climate emergency.  STOP WHAT YOU’RE DOING: New rules limiting MPs’ second jobs come into force from tomorrow. No confirmation of MPs planning to quit over the change yet, as reported by the Times, but Playbook PM’s ears are always open.  BLAIRING ON: The real-life Tony Blair (as opposed to a terrifying AI version) splashed the latest London Standard as the promo for his book “On Leadership” released almost two months ago continued. The ex-PM slammed the criticism of Labour peer Waheed Alli — who he ennobled in 1998 — claiming “he’s never asked for anything from the Labour Party” and is “one of the most decent people you could ever meet.” Which is nice.  Do I detect a hint of jealousy? Blair also he was baffled by his former spinner Alastair Campbell’s podcasting fame: “It’s incredible, I mean, him selling out the O2. I’m, well, amazed!” Campbell had a light-hearted pop back at his old boss on X.  DEFECTION — SORTA: The Express’ Christian Calgie reports that Reform U.K. has welcomed Tory councillor Jaymey McIvor to the cause, after leader Farage wrote to local politicians last night advising ’em to cross the floor or lose their seats. But it isn’t quite a defection … since McIvor was expelled from the Tories earlier this month after facing a disciplinary investigation and hearing.  Two more: Reform U.K. is also touting the capture of two new Tory councillors in Scotland, as the party eyes a Holyrood breakthrough after its surprisingly good election result up north.  OH, MARY LOU: In Ireland, the road to re-election just got harder for Sinn Féin Leader Mary Lou McDonald, after one of the country’s most prominent hard-left politicians, ex-MEP Clare Daly, announced she would run against McDonald in her inner-city Dublin power base, POLITICO’s Irish correspondent Shawn Pogatchnik writes.  Anti-everything Clare: Well known internationally for her anti-NATO and anti-Israel stances, Daly narrowly lost her European Parliament seat in June’s elections. Now she aims to win one of the four Irish parliamentary seats up for grabs in Dublin Central. Daly will seek to likely to hoover anti-establishment votes away from McDonald. A snap election is widely expected to be called in the next few weeks.  AROUND THE WORLD  IN RUSSIA: Britain condemned Moscow’s “shameful behavior” after diplomats including Deputy Ambassador Tom Dodd were targeted at Vnukovo airport in the capital. Dodd was swarmed by a group claiming to be protestors and journalists when he landed with colleagues. A Foreign Office spokesperson told the Telegraph: “Intimidation will not deter our staff from promoting international stability and U.K. interests around the world.”  At the BRICS summit: U.N. Secretary General Antonio Guterres told President Vladimir Putin a “just peace” was needed to end the war in Ukraine. Visiting Russia for the first time in more than two years, Guterres urged Putin to sign a peace deal “in line with the U.N. Charter, international law and U.N. General Assembly resolutions.” Sky has further details.  MIDDLE EAST LATEST: Turkey launched a second day of successive airstrikes in Iraq and Syria after five people were killed and 22 injured in an apparent terror attack on Ankara. The Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) was immediately blamed for the attack, despite no group claiming responsibility, with PKK “strategic locations” including military, intelligence and energy facilities hit. More from the Times.  While in Gaza: At least 17 Palestinians including children were killed by an Israeli strike on a school in Nuseirat camp, where residents displaced by fighting had sheltered. The Israeli military said the hit targeted a Hamas command and control center in a compound formerly used as a school. Reuters has a write-up.  FROM BRUSSELS: The EU will release €799 million in grants to Slovakia after a long-standing dispute over threats to the rule of law. The payment had previously been blocked by the European Commission to put pressure on Prime Minister Robert Fico after he made attempts to control the media and said pro-Kremlin rhetoric. My colleague Elisa Braun has an explainer.  **A message from Lloyds Banking Group: Together with the National Wealth Fund, we are delivering £500m in funding to support the retrofit of social homes across the UK. It is estimated that close to £36 billion of investment will be needed to bring housing association properties to EPC C by 2030. These loans will help provide upgrades such as low carbon heating and insulation, creating warmer homes, lower bills and better life outcomes for social housing residents. At Lloyds Banking Group, we have championed the social housing sector for decades, providing over £18.5 billion in new funding to the sector since 2018. This initiative will reduce carbon emissions, lower energy bills, and create warmer, healthier homes. Find out more about our efforts to support sustainable housing here.**  TONIGHT’S MEDIA ROUND  LEADING THE NEWS BULLETINS: Channel 5 News (5 p.m.) leads on serial killer Lucy Letby being refused permission to appeal by the Court of Appeal … BBC News at Six focuses on the Commonwealth heads of government meeting … Channel 4 News (7 p.m.) looks at special educational needs provision and has an interview with Chancellor Rachel Reeves in Washington.
