text: Good afternoon. This is Andrew McDonald, with Dan Bloom aboard a plane to Samoa and Noah Keate ably assisting from Westminster.  WEDNESDAY CHEAT SHEET  — Labour spent its day trying to hose down Donald Trump’s claims of foreign election interference.  — Keir Starmer, on the plane to Samoa, again insisted there would be no deal on reparations for slavery.  — All the gossip and pain from the plane as the grueling flight to Samoa reaches its 21st hour.  — Bezzie mates John Healey and Boris Pistorius signed a defense pact in London.  — Yvette Cooper announced a new “presumption of anonymity” for firearms cops facing prosecution for shootings.  — There’s a new feline in Downing Street.  **A message from Lloyds Banking Group: At Lloyds Banking Group we believe everyone deserves a safe space to call home. Our new research with national homelessness charity Crisis shows that nearly three-quarters of people spoken to on social housing waiting lists are living in unsuitable properties that negatively impact their health. Find out more here.**  TOP OF THE NEWSLIST  TRUMPED-UP CHARGES: The government wanted to talk about the Commonwealth summit Keir Starmer is still on his way to … or its shiny new defense pact … or even its reform of the water industry. But instead, it’s still firefighting a diplomatic row over Labour troops heading out to campaign against Donald Trump.  Recap: Keir Starmer’s Labour Party was formally accused last night of breaking U.S. electoral law through “blatant foreign interference.” The row centers around a now-deleted LinkedIn post from Labour’s Head of Operations Sofia Patel, in which she said she had nearly 100 “current (and former) party staff” ready to campaign for Kamala Harris in several swing states — and advertising for more to join. Foreign nationals are permitted to volunteer in U.S. campaigns as long as they are not compensated.  Labour insists … that where Labour activists are taking part in this campaigning, “they do so at their own expense, in accordance with the laws and rules,” a spokesperson said. The party insists too that they are not organizing or funding anyone going over, and that accommodation is being provided by volunteers.  Trying to answer more questions: Labour also said the presence of top aides Morgan McSweeney and Matthew Doyle — both named in the legal letter — at the Democratic National Convention in August was normal, as the party sends a delegation to every Democratic convention. McSweeney’s costs were met by the Labour Party, but the argument is that neither he or Doyle were doing anything to assist or advise the Harris campaign.  To be fair: It’s also true to say this kind of sister-party campaigning has been going on for years, and that there are numerous examples of high-profile Tories doing the same thing. No one seems to care that Scottish Lib Dem Leader Alex Cole-Hamilton is over in Pennsylvania, either.  But the problem is: Whether there’s anything to the Trump team’s audacious argument that Patel’s offer to “sort your housing” amounts to a broader, foreign national contribution for the Harris campaign rather than just volunteering — opinions vary — the row has triggered allies of the thin-skinned dude who might end up on the other side of the special relationship from January. And Starmer’s own lieutenants have spent a precious day having to field questions about it.  We’ll still be special pals: “This happens in every election, it’s commonplace,” Defense Secretary John Healey insisted after hailing a new defense pact with Germany (more on that below). “It is very different to the determination of the Labour government to work with whoever American people elect next month as their president … that’s a relationship that exists with the political ups and downs on both sides to be Atlantic, and we’re determined to make that work.”  Earlier on: Starmer insisted he had established a “good relationship” with Trump when he had dinner with him last month, in quotes from the plane covered by this morning’s Playbook.  Elsewhere in London: Jokingly asked at DPMQs by SNP chief Stephen Flynn if she’d join him in applauding “brave Labour staff members” for campaigning against the Donald, Deputy PM Angela Rayner stuck to the line of staff doing “what they want to do in their own time with their own money.”  Reminder: Foreign Secretary David Lammy and his team have spent months and months trying to woo Trump and his team.  Obviously: Trump ally Nigel Farage — no stranger to a bit of campaigning in the U.S. — is leading the attacks on Starmer this side of the Atlantic. Farage said Starmer had “insulted the incoming Trump administration”. My POLITICO colleagues have more from Nige.  Plus: A couple of Tory MPs are poking their heads above the parapet to have a pop, with one telling my colleague Noah Keate that Labour didn’t “grasp that they are in government now, which demands a different standard. It’s student politics stuff.” Another, the MP Neil Shastri-Hurst, told Noah he was “deeply uncomfortable with the concept of the Labour Party organizing for their staff to move en bloc to back one candidate over another in the U.S.” Labour denies that charge, obvs.  So far: That’s about where the backlash at the U.K.-side ends, and the row is unlikely to hurt Labour much domestically — since Trump is still well unpopular in the U.K. But Trump famously has quite the long memory when it comes to beefs and spats.  Or maybe not that long a memory: The now-moaning Trump campaign in 2016 actually sent emails to British MPs begging for money, which, if any donated, would have counted as … foreign election interference. Former SNP MP Stuart McDonald shared some of those emails with Playbook PM.  In one email … dated 21 June 2016, Trump promised to “personally match every dollar that comes in within the next 48 hours up to $2 million.” He goes on: “Stuart, this means any donation you make between $1 and $2,700 (the maximum allowable contribution) will be matched, dollar-for-dollar.”  MOVING FORWARD ON THE PLANE  NO DEAL: Keir Starmer wants Commonwealth nations to “face forward” rather than drawing him into “very, very long endless discussions” about reparations, Playbook’s Dan Bloom writes from the plane to Samoa. The prime minister was asked during the flight to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Samoa about Caribbean nations’ calls for slavery reparations.  The quotes: “I think we should be facing forward,” he told hacks, insisting Commonwealth nations were “most interested” in reforming financial institutions and dealing with climate change. He added: “That’s where I’m going to put my focus rather than what will end up being very, very long endless discussions about reparations on the past.” Fuller quotes should be popping up shortly.  TBF: No one really believes the U.K. will hand over reparations worth anywhere from £200 billion to £18 trillion, depending on whose maths you use. For many — including candidates for the post of Commonwealth secretary-general — the conversation about reparations is already couched in terms of climate action. But one U.K. official predicts the atmosphere could be “febrile.”  Starmer also … insisted CHOGM is “very important,” despite several members going to the Russian-Chinese BRICS-fest instead (see this morning’s Playbook). “Look, that’s a matter for them as to where they attend,” Starmer said. He added he’ll be using the summit to “focus on growth and trade.”  POSTCARD FROM THE PACIFIC: We’re into hour 21 of the PM’s grueling 28-hour journey to Samoa, an alarmingly bleary-eyed Dan writes. The plane is on its final refueling stop in Hawaii and its inhabitants have just been allowed onto tarmac for the first time, and are doing jumping jacks as the Hawaiian sunrise approaches, the first natural light since leaving the U.K. The airline handed out anti-DVT compression socks, while Starmer himself arrived already in trainers, a sleek black zip-up top and a white T-shirt. Thankfully, aides decided to pass on the usual huddle photo. Everyone has been sleeping forever, yet is knackered. All we know is the plane now. There is no world other than the plane.  Consolation prize: Justin Trudeau may not have made it to CHOGM, but a representative for the Canadian PM did deliver sickly-sweet donuts to Starmer’s plane during an overnight refueling stop in Winnipeg. Starmer made a brisk visit down the cabin to hand them out to the traveling pack before we all conked out again.  One eye on Blighty: Starmer is accompanied to CHOGM by his new Deputy Chief of Staff Jill Cuthbertson, though not chief of staff Morgan McSweeney, which may be sensible given the number of domestic fish to fry. A few weeks ago No. 10 axed its original plan to tack on a visit to Australia, as it would have kept Starmer abroad for too long before the budget.  Still to come: Starmer will kick off an afternoon of pre-summit activities in Samoa while you’re sleeping tonight, with a visit to sailors on HMS Tamar — which aided a New Zealand navy ship that sank spilling 200,000 liters of diesel — and meetings with business leaders, followed by a state banquet. King Charles is doing his state visit to Samoa at the same time, though Dan hears the king isn’t due at the banquet (which is hosted by the Samoan PM).  CHOGM SCOOP: Some African nations are expected to apply renewed pressure this week for Zimbabwe to rejoin the Commonwealth, three people with knowledge of summit planning tell Dan and Esther Webber. Harare was suspended in 2002 (and withdrew a year later) under the late “tyrant” president Robert Mugabe, but has been trying to rejoin since 2018.  Might this be one? Manoah Esipisu, Kenya’s High Commissioner to London for six years until May, told Dan: “African members have been a little impatient about what they see as unnecessary delays in this process.”  But but but … Nations are *still* awaiting a full report by Commonwealth observers on Zimbabwe’s 2023 general election, which re-elected president Emmerson Mnangagwa after he took over from Mugabe in a 2017 coup. Human Rights Watch said the poll was “characterized by repression of civil and political rights.” A Commonwealth spokesperson told Dan: “The report is in the final stages of publication and will be released imminently. We confirm that all necessary procedures have been followed.”  Not holding back: Stuart Mole of the Institute of Commonwealth Studies told Dan the treatment of the report had been a “scandalous and in clear violation” of guidelines, as the requirement to publish in a timely way had been “blatantly ignored.”  **Exclusive POLITICO Pro access for House of Lords members and staff. The ultimate platform for political professionals, offering premium access to data, policy analysis, and breaking news. Do you want to have access to the trial? It’s available for all House of Lords members, staffers, researchers, and more. Contact your Librarian Office or email [email protected] to claim your trial access.**  THE LIGHTHOUSE PACT  LABOUR’S FAVE BORIS: Defense Secretary John Healey and his German counterpart Boris Pistorius bigged each other and the Germany-U.K. relationship up as they signed their much-trailed defense pact in London this morning. Playbook PM was there.  I’ve always pictured them in a lighthouse: The pair signed the new Trinity House Agreement at the plush Trinity House in London — the old building in charge of lighthouses. Soldiers in uniform milled around mixing in one room, with the media penned into another, before a press conference this morning. A grand portrait of Samuel Pepys — former master of the House — stared down at media waiting for the Boris and John show.  Holy trinity: The pact includes joint missile development and extra exercises in the Baltics … hosting rights for submarine-hunting planes in Scotland … and a major artillery factory deal for Düsseldorf-based weapons-maker Rheinmetall. POLITICO’s Joshua Posaner and Esther Webber had a good read on the context this morning.  Trump-proofing: In their quick speeches and answers to questions from U.K. and German press, both men emphazised the importance of Europe learning to look after itself — in a world where the United States is more, err, unpredictable. “We have to do more, because the U.S. will shift their focus more to the Indo-Pacific for reasons we all know,” Pistorius said. “So it is a question of: Will they do much less in Europe because of that, or only a bit less?”  And therefore: “[We need to do] what we both say: European nations taking more responsibility for the heavy lifting and the leadership within the NATO alliance,” Healey added. As two of the higher spending European nations on defense, the subtext for other allies is fairly obvious.  The lads … were in lockstep, with Pistorius gazing lovingly at Healey while he spoke and vice versa. Pistorius cracked a joke about his wife thinking he sees the defense secretary more than her.  Are they actually pals? Yes, it seems. Anne McElvoy, host of the Power Play podcast, caught up with Healey beforehand. Healey said his close working relationship with Pistorius was key to getting the deal over the line in four months instead of the intended six — and that they managed some downtime together too. “Of course we’ve had a beer together,” he quipped. But, all importantly, was it German or British, Anne asked. “Well it was definitely a Pilsner. I can’t remember where it was brewed.” The full podcast will be out tomorrow morning.  ** Chancellor Rachel Reeves will deliver her first Budget on October 30. Our policy experts will unpack what that means for your industry. Join our sessions on Technology, Trade, Financial Services or Energy & Climate on October 31.**  DRIVETIME DEBRIEF  CLOSING RANKS: Firearms officers facing prosecution for shootings in the line of duty will get a “presumption of anonymity” up to the point of convictions, Yvette Cooper told the Commons as part of a suite of measures to quell police anger over the trial of Martyn Blake, my Playbook colleague Sam Blewett writes in. Top brass have been pushing for greater protections for the rank-and-file after the marksman was cleared of murdering alleged gang member Chris Kaba. They’ll welcome the home secretary’s announcement that the measure will be included in the upcoming Crime and Policing Bill — but justice and transparency campaigners surely won’t.  A shot in the dark: Since 2005 there have been only two prosecutions of firearms officers — but officials fear even this small number is enough to create a widespread chilling effect. Sam hears Cooper isn’t considering extending anonymity to cops who aren’t marksmen. In addition to the anonymity move, a three-month review has been launched into whether the bar should be raised for determining the use of force in misconduct cases, and Attorney General Richard Hermer has asked the director of public prosecutions to review CPS guidance over charging police officers.  Sweetening the pill: The Home Office is also promising to overhaul the vetting of police officers — a key recommendation of a review into how an off-duty officer committed the abduction, rape and murder of Sarah Everard. The department wants to introduce legislation that’d make it easier for police chiefs to dismiss dodgy cops found guilty of gross misconduct and of those who lack vetting. Officials argue the current guidance has been over-focused on police assets and intelligence, rather than protecting public safety.  DOWDEN’S LAST HURRAH: Angela Rayner made her debut appearance answering deputy PMQs for the government this lunchtime. Up against Oliver Dowden, serious questions about the budget and, here’s a surprise, what counts as a working person quickly gave way to a love-in as the shadow deputy leader of the opposition is expected to depart the role when Rishi Sunak steps down as Tory leader next month. Rayner said she would “miss our exchanges” which she called “the battle of the gingers.”  Get a room: Dowden, a staunch royalist, referenced how the Commonwealth was “brought together by historical and cultural ties, indeed, much like the pair of us.” Rayner shot him a love heart — where’s Richard Curtis when you need him? POLITICO’s Noah Keate penned the scorecard, and ruled that love won the day. Next week’s PMQs risks being just as sycophantic, as Sunak bows out. At least there are the budget clashes to look forward too.  CONSTRUCTIVE CRITICISM: Rachel Reeves said Cabinet colleagues raising complaints about their budgets next week was a “constructive process,” insisting they “understand the challenges that we face as a government.” Reeves was speaking to Matt Chorley’s BBC 5 live show. Chorley has tweeted out the best lines here.  The chancellor also revealed … that she and Jeremy Hunt WhatsApp regularly. It’s a love-in kinda day.  WATERWORKS: On a busy day in Westminster, Environment Sec Steve Reed announced his big review of the water sector — to be chaired by former Deputy Governor of the Bank of England Jon Cunliffe. The review will focus on regulation of the industry and reform of Ofwat — and basically look at everything except nationalization, which Labour is keen to insist is firmly off the table.  MORE PRESSURE: Some Labour MPs are urging the government to take a tougher stance on Israel, after the killing of Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar last week failed to end the conflict in Gaza. And it’s not just the usual suspects. “Ultimately, there’s a limit to how many half measures you can deploy,” Peter Lamb, who’s not a Socialist Campaign Group member and opposed Jeremy Corbyn’s leadership, told PoliticsHome‘s Nadine Batchelor-Hunt and Sienna Rodgers. “If Israel does not want to listen to anyone else on human rights questions, then our obligation to supply them with armaments in order to defend themselves doesn’t really exist.”  HORRIBLE NEWS IN THE CHANNEL: Three migrants drowned in the English Channel after their boat capsized about two kilometers off the Calais coast, the French authorities confirmed. Another 48 people were rescued. The total number of people who have died crossing the Channel this year now stands at at least 55, the highest figure ever recorded. The Times has more.  LESS DEATH, MORE ASSISTING: The divisions assisted dying creates across and within parties were laid bare as Wes Streeting confirmed he would vote against Labour MP Kim Leadbeater’s private members’ bill. Speaking to LBC’s Shelagh Fogarty, the health secretary said “we can’t pretend that there won’t be a cost to all of this,” as he called for a focus on the ways existing end of life care can be a form of assisted dying.  Not doing God: Streeting, who’s a Christian, also criticized those who claimed he was imposing his faith on others. “I’ve never talked about this issue in the context of my own faith,” he said. “Actually, I’m a bit sick of the soft bigotry.” If you fancy hearing more about religion and politics … POLITICO’s own Sascha O’Sullivan explored the issue for Westminster Insider earlier this month.  SOCIAL (MEDIA) AFFAIRS  Don’t ask don’t get: Fair play to Times Radio producer Oli Mansfield for using Elon Musk’s own realm to try and bag an interview with the billionaire.  AROUND THE WORLD  MIDDLE EAST LATEST: Israel carried out four strikes in the ancient Lebanese city of Tyre, hours after expanding its evacuation orders. The city contains UNESCO World Heritage-listed Roman ruins and is one of the oldest continually inhabited cities in the world. There were no reports of casualties but Mortada Mhanna, who leads Tyre’s disaster management unit, said “the situation is very bad.” The Times has more information.  In Israel: The Iron Dome system downed rockets launched by Hezbollah at Tel Aviv above U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken’s hotel. Blinken and other U.S. officials sheltered downstairs before heading to Saudi Arabia — via the Telegraph.  OUT OF NORTH KOREA: America and NATO have “evidence” North Korean troops have been deployed to Russia, U.S. Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin said Wednesday. Austin added that if the troops fought on behalf of Moscow in Ukraine, “that is a very, very serious issue, and it will have impacts not only on in Europe — It will also impact things in the Indo Pacific as well.” More from my colleagues Csongor Körömi and Stuart Lau.  IN RUSSIA: BRICS leaders including President Vladimir Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi used their summit to call for a cease-fire in Gaza, and made positive noises about a non-Western payment system. Ukraine was mentioned only once in the final communique. Reuters has further details.  IN FRANCE: Gisèle Pelicot took the stand in court as her former husband Dominique was on trial for drugging and raping her when they were married, and inviting dozens of men to rape her while she was unconscious. Pelicot said she was “completely destroyed” but wanted to tell other women who had been raped: “It’s not for us to have shame — it’s for them.” The BBC has a writeup.  **A message from Lloyds Banking Group: Across the UK, over 1.5 million people are on social housing waiting lists. Research shows that one in four people on social housing waiting lists report feel hopeless, part of a whole A-Z of problems no family should have to experience. Together with national homelessness charity Crisis, our new campaign documents the lived experience of those on social housing waiting lists, highlighting the importance of our call for a million more homes at social rent by 2033. Find out more here. **  TONIGHT’S MEDIA ROUND  LEADING THE NEWS BULLETINS: Channel 5 News (5 p.m.) leads on the death of three people at a Dorset care home after a suspected carbon monoxide leak … Channel 4 News (7 p.m.) focuses on Home Secretary Yvette Cooper’s announcement that firearms officers will get a presumption of anonymity.
